_readme: Amiga Constellation — canonical data file. Everything the site shows lives here.
HOW TO EDIT: change this JSON (or the amiga-data.js sidecar next to the HTML,
which contains the same object) and reload the page. Field guide:
entry.id         unique slug; 'related' lists refer to these ids
entry.year       first public release/announcement year (sets the era)
entry.category   one of meta.groups[].cats[].id
entry.kind       one of meta.kinds[].id
entry.status     one of meta.statuses[].id
entry.arch       any of meta.architectures[].id (first one = primary)
entry.weight     1-5 significance; 5 = 'Essentials only' landmark
entry.what/why   description and significance; entry.version = detail line
entry.url        verified official page (omit if none); entry.unverified flags shaky facts
entry.image      OPTIONAL picture for the entry's plate. Any of:
an absolute URL   'https://example.org/a500.jpg'
a file beside the HTML  './images/a500.jpg'  or  'images/a500.jpg'
an inline data: URI (keeps the site a single file)
Omit it and the entry keeps its hand-drawn pictogram. If the URL
fails to load — offline, moved, blocked — the pictogram shows
instead, so a bad link can never leave a broken frame.
entry.imageCredit  OPTIONAL source/licence line, shown in the detail drawer
entry.imageFit     OPTIONAL CSS object-fit override: cover (default) or contain
entry.imagePosition OPTIONAL CSS object-position override, e.g. 50% 20%
entry.imageBackground OPTIONAL plate background for transparent/contained images
entry.related    ids this entry descends from (children are derived automatically)
domains = graph clusters for the default view; tours = guided story routes.
Snapshot: research verified August 2026.

theses.title: The original machines became platforms, not products
theses.body: The A2000, A3000 and A4000 were designed around internal expansion; the A500, A600 and A1200 grew sidecar, CPU-socket and trapdoor ecosystems. That openness let later generations replace nearly every subsystem — processor, graphics, storage, video output, networking, USB, even parts of the chipset model.

theses.title: The future split rather than ending
theses.body: No single successor inherited everything. AmigaOS 4 preserved the official API lineage on PowerPC; MorphOS built a separate system and colonised used Apple hardware; AROS pursued open re-implementation across architectures; FPGA and replica projects preserved hardware behaviour; emulators preserved access. The branches compete — and together they explain the longevity.

theses.title: Emulation became infrastructure
theses.body: UAE did not stay one application. Its descendants are desktop emulators, Raspberry Pi engines, libretro cores, netplay systems, commercial preservation packages — and the hidden foundation of retail devices. Amiberry and WinUAE-derived code now sits underneath environments whose users never perceive an emulator at all.

theses.title: FPGA changed the meaning of compatibility
theses.body: Minimig began as an open A500 recreation; MiST, MiSTer, Analogue Pocket and FPGA Arcade extended it toward AGA. Apollo’s 68080 and SAGA take the revisionist path instead — adding instructions, graphics capability and whole system designs while keeping a 68k software world. "Compatible" now spans faithful recreation through deliberate extension.

theses.title: Curation matters as much as accuracy
theses.body: A bare emulator plus a ROM is not an approachable system. Amiga Forever solves legality and configuration; AmiKit, ClassicWB and BetterWB curate desktops; Icaros packaged AROS; Pimiga and Amibian make Pi appliances; AmigaVision targets repeatable preservation across real hardware, FPGA and emulators. These projects preserve workflows and context, not only instruction sets.

theses.title: The desktop was always replaceable
theses.body: Workbench is iconic, but Amiga users routinely swapped file managers, console handlers, shells, toolkits, icons and the entire desktop. Directory Opus Magellan, Scalos, Ambient and Wanderer show the platform identity sits below any one visual shell — which is how descendants stayed recognisably Amiga-like while developing distinct interfaces.

cautions.title: Availability changes fast
cautions.body: Small-run boards move between shipping, pre-order, waiting-list and unavailable without announcements.

cautions.title: Release years are fuzzy
cautions.body: Announcement, developer-board, first-batch and general-retail dates often differ. Years here are first public release.

cautions.title: Compatibility is configuration-specific
cautions.body: MorphOS on Apple hardware depends on the exact model and GPU; AmigaOS 4 depends on the listed board or accelerator.

cautions.title: FPGA is not automatically cycle-perfect
cautions.body: FPGA cores can be extremely faithful but remain engineering models with their own limits.

cautions.title: Curated images may carry licensing constraints
cautions.body: Anything needing AmigaOS, Kickstart ROMs or commercial software should be built from legally obtained files. Listing a project is not an endorsement of any download bundle.

cautions.title: Ownership is a separate map
cautions.body: Technical lineage and corporate rights are different things. See the Ownership & brand category.

entries.name: Lorraine prototype
entries.what: The pre-Commodore development system built by Jay Miner's team that established the chipset-led architecture later sold as the Amiga 1000.
entries.why: Graphics, audio and pre-emptive multitasking were conceived as one integrated system from the start. The Boing Ball demo ran on a Lorraine at CES in January 1984.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Kaiiv, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Amiga 1000
entries.what: The first shipping Amiga: 68000 at 7.16 MHz, OCS chipset, 256 KB RAM, and Kickstart loaded from disk into writable control store.
entries.why: Turned Lorraine into a consumer computer and set the software and expansion conventions everything else followed.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected source — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Ranger prototype
entries.what: An unreleased advanced-chipset and high-end system effort developed between the A1000 and the later big-box machines.
entries.why: A reminder that Amiga evolution included ambitious internal branches that never became products.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Trafalgarcircle; retouch: Ubcule, public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Amiga 2000
entries.what: The expandable desktop Amiga: five Zorro II slots, a CPU slot, a video slot and ISA pass-throughs.
entries.why: Its open slots made it the platform for Video Toaster systems, accelerators, graphics cards and decades of upgrades.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum
entries.name: Amiga 500
entries.what: The cost-reduced keyboard wedge and best-selling Amiga: 68000, OCS (later ECS Agnus), 512 KB, with a trapdoor and side expansion bus.
entries.why: The mass-market foundation — most people's mental image of an Amiga, and the target of an enormous games and demo library.

entries.imageCredit: User-provided image — August 2026
entries.name: Amiga 2500
entries.what: Factory A2000 configurations bundled with an A2620 (68020) or A2630 (68030) accelerator and SCSI.
entries.why: It formalised the community's favourite idea: start with an expandable Amiga and grow it into a workstation.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amiga 1500 — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga 1500
entries.what: A UK-market A2000 variant commonly supplied with two floppy drives and no hard disk.
entries.why: A region-specific model that became an accessible route into the big-box expansion ecosystem.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Joe Smith; retouch by Ubcule, public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Amiga 3000
entries.what: A compact high-end workstation: 68030 at 16/25 MHz with FPU, ECS plus the Amber flicker-fixer for 31 kHz output, Zorro III, on-board SCSI and SIMM sockets.
entries.why: Often regarded as the most coherent big-box design, and a durable base for 68060, PowerPC and RTG builds.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected source — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga 3000UX
entries.what: A3000 configurations sold with Commodore's Amiga UNIX (SVR4) rather than only AmigaOS.
entries.why: It showed the same hardware could serve as a Unix workstation, even without AmigaOS application compatibility.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected source — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga 3500 prototype
entries.what: A pre-production tower form of the A3000, associated with workstation and UNIX plans.
entries.why: It led into the production A3000T and illustrates Commodore's workstation ambitions.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected source — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga 3000T
entries.what: Tower version of the A3000 with additional room for drives and expansion.
entries.why: One of the rarest production big-box Amigas and a favoured platform for serious expansion.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amiga 500 Plus — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga 500 Plus
entries.what: An ECS revision of the A500 with 1 MB chip RAM, Kickstart 2.04 and a battery-backed clock — the infamous leaking barrel battery.
entries.why: A short-lived but important bridge from OCS-era software toward the A600 generation.

entries.imageCredit: User-provided image — August 2026
entries.name: Commodore CDTV
entries.what: An A500-based multimedia CD player in a hi-fi case, with CD-ROM and the DMAC controller, running Kickstart 1.3 plus a CDTV extended ROM.
entries.why: It anticipated CD-based consoles and demonstrated that Amiga technology could leave the desktop.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Ajne01, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Amiga 600
entries.what: The smallest classic wedge (project "A300"): 68000, ECS, and the Gayle chip providing internal 44-pin IDE and a PCMCIA slot, but no numeric keypad.
entries.why: Its compact surface-mount board — notorious for capacitor leakage — later became a surprising favourite for Vampire and PiStorm transformations.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Wojciech Pędzich, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Amiga 1200
entries.what: The affordable AGA wedge: 68EC020 at 14 MHz, Alice/Lisa AGA chips, Gayle IDE and PCMCIA, 2 MB chip RAM, a 150-pin trapdoor with a real 32-bit bus, and a clockport.
entries.why: Its balance of compatibility, AGA graphics and expandability made it the centre of the modern classic scene.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Old Crap Vintage Computing
entries.name: Amiga 4000
entries.what: The flagship AGA desktop: 68EC030 at 25 MHz or 68040 on a CPU daughtercard, Zorro III via Super Buster, IDE and SIMM RAM.
entries.why: The principal high-end AGA platform, and the classic machine most often pushed into 060, PowerPC and RTG territory.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected source — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: CDTV-CR prototype
entries.what: A cost-reduced second-generation CDTV design that did not reach normal production.
entries.why: It connects the original CDTV experiment to Commodore's later CD32 console strategy.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Evan-Amos, public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Amiga CD32
entries.what: A CD-based AGA console: 68EC020 at 14 MHz, 2 MB chip RAM, double-speed CD and the Akiko chip combining CD control with chunky-to-planar conversion.
entries.why: Commodore's last major consumer launch became a preservation and homebrew target in its own right, and its expansion connector allows full-computer upgrades.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected source — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AAA chipset
entries.what: A 64-bit next-generation chipset ("Andrea, Linda, Mary, Monica") with 16-bit audio and chunky modes. Silicon existed but was never debugged to production; cancelled in 1993.
entries.why: The successor that would have answered the PC's graphics advance — and the clearest measure of what Commodore's collapse cost technically.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Hombre chipset — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Hombre chipset
entries.what: A PA-RISC-based 3D chipset and console project with Windows NT ambitions, killed by Commodore's 1994 bankruptcy.
entries.why: Commodore's final attempt at a generational leap, abandoning the 68k line entirely.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amiga 4000T — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga 4000T
entries.what: The tower flagship with added SCSI, produced first by Commodore and then by Escom's Amiga Technologies in 1995–96.
entries.why: The final production classic model, roomy enough for the most extreme accelerator, graphics and storage builds.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amiga Technologies relaunch — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga Technologies relaunch
entries.what: After Commodore's liquidation, Escom's Amiga Technologies (Petro Tyschtschenko) restarted A1200 and A4000T manufacture.
entries.why: It kept new classic hardware on sale and briefly connected the Commodore era to post-bankruptcy stewardship.

entries.imageCredit: User-provided image — August 2026
entries.name: Amiga Walker prototype
entries.what: Amiga Technologies' planned mid-range successor — 68EC030, AGA, and a distinctive expandable case — shown publicly but cancelled after Escom's collapse.
entries.why: Its famous vacuum-cleaner-like case became the visual symbol of the product path that almost continued.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Tord and Valeria Magnussen / Amiga Hardware Database
entries.name: MacroSystem DraCo
entries.what: A professional Amiga-compatible non-linear video editing workstation: 68060 (some 68040) at 50 MHz, unified memory to 128 MB, and no Commodore custom chipset at all. It ran AmigaOS 3.1 from an A3000 Kickstart with a modified SetPatch, driving MacroSystem's MovieShop software over the proprietary DraCoBus.
entries.why: Built in roughly nine months by about sixteen engineers reacting to Commodore's bankruptcy, DraCo proved AmigaOS could survive on clean-room, RTG-oriented hardware — conceptually the direct ancestor of the AmigaOne, Sam and X5000 idea. Supported commercially to 2000; the cheaper Casablanca appliance followed.

entries.name: phase5 A\BOX
entries.what: phase5's ambitious planned PowerPC successor, built around a custom "Caipirinha" chipset. It never shipped, and phase5 entered insolvency around 1999–2000.
entries.why: Its ideas and team history foreshadowed the post-Commodore split into PowerPC boards and new operating systems — several of the same people went on to bplan, Pegasos and MorphOS.

entries.name: BoXeR motherboard
entries.what: A long-running attempt at an updated single-board classic-compatible computer: 68040/68060, AGA-compatible, PCI, in ATX form. Repeatedly announced across roughly 1997–2003 and never reaching volume production.
entries.why: The canonical example of the community's recurring wish for a genuinely new classic-chipset motherboard — a wish answered instead by FPGA recreations, ReAmiga replicas and the AA3000+.

entries.name: Apple Power Mac G4 family
entries.what: Selected Radeon-equipped Power Mac G4 towers and the Cube are supported by MorphOS.
entries.why: They offer abundant, repairable expansion hardware for an OS whose purpose-built machines are rare and expensive.

entries.name: Apple PowerBook / iBook G4
entries.what: Supported Radeon-equipped G4 laptops give MorphOS a portable hardware branch.
entries.why: A community port delivered something classic Amiga never had as a production product: a practical laptop.

entries.name: AmigaOne SE
entries.what: Eyetech's first shipping AmigaOne board, using a Mai Logic Teron design with a soldered PowerPC 750CXe at 600 MHz.
entries.why: It made the AmigaOne name concrete and gave AmigaOS 4 developers real PowerPC target hardware.

entries.name: bplan Pegasos I
entries.what: The first Pegasos MicroATX board, designed by ex-phase5 engineers Gerald Carda and Thomas Knäbel, using a G3 CPU card and the MAI Articia S northbridge whose DMA bug forced the "April" fix chip.
entries.why: It established the "blue" PowerPC branch: Amiga-like APIs and experience on non-Amiga hardware, closely tied to early MorphOS.

entries.name: AmigaOne XE
entries.what: The expandable ATX AmigaOne, taking CPU cards up to a G4 at 933 MHz, with four PCI slots and AGP.
entries.why: For many early adopters this was the practical start of daily AmigaOS 4 use.

entries.name: Apple Power Mac G5
entries.what: Selected Power Mac 7,2 and 7,3 systems are fully supported by MorphOS.
entries.why: They provide the fastest widely available used desktop hardware in the MorphOS ecosystem.

entries.imageCredit: Hardware photo: AmigaOS.net
entries.name: bplan Pegasos II
entries.what: A refined Pegasos board replacing Articia with the Marvell Discovery II, taking G3 600 MHz or G4 1.0 GHz cards. ACube later sold AmigaOS 4.1 for it; Hyperion moved that to digital download in 2025.
entries.why: One of the rare bridge machines where both major PowerPC Amiga-like operating systems meet, and still a supported MorphOS 3.20 target.

entries.name: Apple iMac G5 / eMac
entries.what: Specific Radeon-equipped eMac and iMac G5 (iSight A1145) models are supported by MorphOS.
entries.why: Community driver work transformed sealed mainstream Macs into elegant all-in-one Amiga-like systems.

entries.name: MicroA1-C
entries.what: A compact Mini-ITX AmigaOne variant with integrated graphics and a single PCI slot.
entries.why: It brought the AmigaOS 4 branch into a small-form-factor board years before mini PCs became routine.

entries.name: Apple Mac mini G4
entries.what: Mass-produced Apple hardware supported by MorphOS, now inexpensive on the second-hand market.
entries.why: Community drivers turned common used Macs into the most accessible genuine PowerPC MorphOS systems — arguably the single biggest driver of MorphOS adoption.

entries.name: Genesi EFIKA 5200B
entries.what: A tiny low-power MPC5200B PowerPC board supported by MorphOS, following Genesi's Open Desktop Workstation.
entries.why: It demonstrated how lightweight the MorphOS and Amiga-like stack could be on modest embedded hardware.

entries.name: ACube Sam440ep
entries.what: A compact board built on the AMCC PowerPC 440EP SoC at 533–667 MHz with onboard Radeon M9, officially supported by AmigaOS 4 from 2008.
entries.why: Independent hardware development kept a purchasable AmigaOS 4 path alive after Eyetech withdrew.

entries.name: ACube Sam440ep-flex
entries.what: A more expandable flex-ATX Sam440 variant with PCI slots and later 800 MHz options.
entries.why: It traded the original board's compactness for the expansion culture familiar to classic users.

entries.name: ACube Sam460ex
entries.what: The next ACube generation: AppliedMicro 460EX at 1.10–1.15 GHz with a PCIe x16 slot, supported by AmigaOS 4 and later MorphOS.
entries.why: Another meeting point between the two PowerPC systems, with far more modern expansion than the Sam440.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Adam Kliczek / memoriesstay.com, CC BY-SA 3.0 PL (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: AmigaOne X1000
entries.what: A-EON's premium flagship on the ATX "Nemo" board: a dual-core P.A. Semi PA6T-1682M at 1.8 GHz — orphaned when Apple bought P.A. Semi — plus the Xena XMOS co-processor on a Xorro slot. Launched January 2012.
entries.why: It restored the idea of a bespoke flagship and funded a new wave of next-gen software and driver work. Community Linux builds for it still appeared in 2026.

entries.name: AmigaOne 500
entries.what: A complete desktop system built around a Sam460ex in a Micro-ATX case, badged with the classic checkmark.
entries.why: It packaged the next-gen branch as a ready-to-use computer rather than a bare specialist board.

entries.name: ACube Sam460cr
entries.what: A cost-reduced Sam460 revision supported by AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS.
entries.why: It extended the dual-OS lifespan of the Sam platform.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: Amiga On The Lake / Old School Game Blog
entries.name: AmigaOne X5000/20
entries.what: A-EON's flagship on the Varisys "Cyrus" board: NXP QorIQ P5020 dual-core at 2.0 GHz, running AmigaOS 4.1, MorphOS and PowerPC Linux. Availability is intermittent and the P5020 is end-of-life.
entries.why: The strongest shared hardware link between today's AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS communities.

entries.name: ACube Sam460LE
entries.what: A limited-edition Sam460 re-run at roughly 1.14 GHz, listed with an AmigaOS 4.1 Final Edition OEM licence but frequently out of stock.
entries.why: Its existence shows sustained small-run demand for dedicated AmigaOS 4 hardware.

entries.name: AmigaOne X5000/40
entries.what: A higher-end X5000 configuration using a quad-core NXP P5040, produced in small numbers.
entries.why: It pushes the custom PowerPC AmigaOne branch to its most capable commercial configuration.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: A-EON Technology / Rabbit Hole Computing
entries.name: AmigaOne A1222 Plus
entries.what: The long-delayed entry-level board, announced as "Tabor" in 2015: NXP QorIQ P1022 dual-core e500v2 at 1.2 GHz. Its SPE vector unit replaces a classic PowerPC FPU, requiring FPU emulation and recompiled software — one reason it took nearly a decade to ship.
entries.why: It broadens the current AmigaOS 4 hardware range and drove significant compatibility work through the OS and application stack. Production is ongoing.

entries.name: Mirari T1042
entries.what: A brand-new PowerPC board designed independently of A-EON: NXP QorIQ T1042 (quad e5500, 1.4 GHz), with dual NVMe, SATA, USB 3.x, 8 GB DDR SODIMM, PCIe, and an Efinix Trion FPGA for glue logic. A T2081 variant with AltiVec 2.0 is planned.
entries.why: MorphOS 3.20 introduced official Mirari support in May 2026 — the first brand-new MorphOS hardware in a decade. It shows the next-gen branch is still designing original motherboards rather than only preserving old ones.

entries.name: Armiga
entries.what: A compact dedicated Amiga emulation appliance: an ARM board running UAE, notably offered in a version with a real 3.5-inch floppy drive so owners could read and archive their own original disks.
entries.why: It bridged physical disk collections and modern ARM emulation years before the mini-console wave — the clearest ancestor of the "Amiga as an appliance" category.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: Retro Games Ltd.
entries.name: THEA500 Mini
entries.what: A roughly half-scale Amiga 500 console emulating OCS/ECS and AGA on an ARM SoC, with HDMI 720p, three USB ports, 25 built-in games, save states and WHDLoad sideloading from USB. Ships with an 8-button pad and a recreated tank mouse; the case keyboard is non-functional.
entries.why: It put a licensed, legal, plug-in Amiga on ordinary retail shelves — ROMs licensed from Cloanto — and introduced the platform to a mainstream audience.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for A600GS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: A600GS
entries.what: A small ARM-based games system and 68k-compatible computer running AmiBench V46, a 68k desktop environment over embedded Linux with an optimised emulation layer. Includes licensed Personal Paint 7.4, OctaMED, Final Writer 7.2 and Directory Opus, plus the AmiSphere online service.
entries.why: A turnkey modern Amiga desktop with legally bundled software — the commercial answer to the community distribution images.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for A1200NG — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: A1200NG
entries.what: A drop-in ARM replacement motherboard for original Amiga 1200 cases, running the same AmiBench V46 environment as the A600GS, with internal USB headers, floppy support, HDMI and an optional CPU Boost Kit.
entries.why: It lets an original A1200 case and keyboard become a modern, quiet, reliable machine — the opposite trade to a Vampire or PiStorm.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for THEA1200 — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: THEA1200
entries.what: A full-size Amiga 1200 recreation with a fully working keyboard. Emulates A1200 AGA plus selectable A500 OCS, A600 ECS and CD32 configurations, with HDMI, four USB ports, RTG support for high-resolution Workbench, Workbench included, 25 built-in games and WHDLoad sideloading.
entries.why: Delayed past 2025 by the Hyperion litigation, it became an officially Amiga-branded licensed product on 18 August 2026 following the settlement — the first mainstream Amiga computer in decades.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Electron9, public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Minimig
entries.what: An open-source re-implementation of the Amiga 500 chipset in a Xilinx Spartan-3 FPGA, paired with a real MC68SEC000. Begun January 2005 and released under GPLv3 on 25 July 2007.
entries.why: The blueprint that proved a community could recreate Amiga hardware behaviour in programmable logic. Its code lives on in virtually every Amiga FPGA project since.

entries.name: C-One / Clone-A
entries.what: The C-One "reconfigurable computer" was an ATX FPGA motherboard extensible via swap-in CPU cards; a later Cyclone III extender could run a Minimig port. Clone-A, its cycle-exact OCS re-implementation as drop-in replacement chips, was demonstrated at Breakpoint 2007 but never released commercially.
entries.why: An independent line of FPGA thinking whose know-how fed into Individual Computers' later products.

entries.name: ACube Minimig v1.1
entries.what: The commercially manufactured Minimig revision with increased memory and a faster 68000 option, announced 9 February 2008.
entries.why: It turned an open hardware experiment into something buyable ready-made.

entries.name: Illuwatar Mini-ITX Minimig
entries.what: A Swedish Mini-ITX form-factor Minimig implementation released under the open-source licence.
entries.why: An early sign that the freed Minimig design would be re-spun independently by third parties.

entries.name: Turbo Chameleon 64
entries.what: An FPGA cartridge for the C64 that also works standalone; among its cores is a Minimig OCS/ECS port with a 68020 soft-CPU by Tobias Gubener. V2 hardware arrived in 2020.
entries.why: It carried the Amiga core into the Commodore 8-bit world, showing how portable the Minimig design had become.

entries.name: MCC-216
entries.what: A compact FPGA system marketed as an Amiga-compatible computer, offering Amiga and other Commodore cores among several recreated machines.
entries.why: An early example of the Amiga core becoming part of a portable multi-system product — and a controversial one, as community testing questioned its performance claims and its originality relative to the open Minimig core.

entries.name: FPGA Arcade Replay
entries.what: A high-capacity FPGA board whose Amiga core reached full AGA support, with an optional physical 68060 daughterboard, 256 MB RAM, USB and Ethernet. Replay 1 is discontinued; Replay 2 has been "in the making" since around 2018 and remains unreleased.
entries.why: It moved FPGA Amiga work from basic A500 recreation toward genuine AGA-class capability.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Ingmar's Retroblog
entries.name: MiST
entries.what: A Cyclone III board — named from aMIga + ST — that moved the whole Amiga including the CPU into the FPGA using the TG68 soft-core, carrying Rok Krajnc's Minimig-AGA fork alongside many other computer cores.
entries.why: It made the recreated Amiga a reusable core rather than a single product, and directly inspired MiSTer.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: MiSTer Addons
entries.name: MiSTer FPGA
entries.what: An open multi-system FPGA platform on the Terasic DE10-Nano. Its Minimig-AGA core covers OCS/ECS/AGA with a 68000 or 68020 soft-CPU, up to 2 MB chip plus 384 MB fast RAM, four floppies, four IDE devices including CD-ROM, RTG to 1920×1080, a shared Linux↔Amiga folder and MIDI.
entries.why: For many enthusiasts the reference low-latency, highly configurable Amiga recreation. The clone wave — MiSTer Pi from $125, QMTECH boards, the consolised MiSTer Multisystem 2 at £276 — made it inexpensive.

entries.name: SiDi / SiDi128
entries.what: MiST-firmware-compatible compact boards. The 2023 SiDi128 pairs a larger EP4CE55 FPGA with 128 MB SDRAM, enough for heavier cores including Minimig with AGA.
entries.why: It keeps the MiST software ecosystem alive on current, purchasable hardware.

entries.name: UnAmiga / neptUNO
entries.what: UnAmiga and UnAmiga Reloaded were small Cyclone IV boards built specifically to run Minimig-AGA forks. Their successors are Antonio Villena's multi-core neptUNO and ZXTRES boards (€150–€369), which include Amiga cores among dozens of systems.
entries.why: A distinctly Spanish branch of the FPGA scene that kept producing purpose-built Amiga boards.

entries.name: Analogue Pocket Amiga core
entries.what: A Minimig-derived openFPGA core for the Analogue Pocket handheld — version 0.2.3 in January 2024, with an Analogizer-enabled 0.3.2 following in February 2025.
entries.why: It made a genuinely handheld FPGA Amiga possible, though it remains early compared with MiSTer.

entries.name: NanoMig
entries.what: Minimig ported to the roughly $30 Gowin Tang Nano 20K and larger Tang boards: A500/A1000-class OCS/ECS, up to 2 MB chip and 4 MB fast RAM, Kickstart 1.2–3.x, four floppies, two IDE drives, HDMI out and USB peripherals. No AGA on the TN20K — the FPGA is too small — with an accelerated 68020 mode in progress.
entries.why: It drops the cost of an FPGA Amiga to pocket money, and is fully open source.

entries.name: GBA1000
entries.what: A long-running enhanced A1000 replacement board, predating the current replica wave.
entries.why: The pioneer of the "build a new Amiga motherboard" idea that ReAmiga later industrialised.

entries.name: A500++ replica board
entries.what: A community-redrawn A500 rev 6A motherboard, widely built directly from the published files using period-compatible components.
entries.why: New PCBs rescue battery-damaged systems and make the original chipset maintainable rather than disposable.

entries.name: AA3000+
entries.what: A community motherboard blending A3000 design goals with AGA-era capabilities — effectively finishing the "AGA A3000" branch Commodore abandoned with its A3000+ prototype.
entries.why: The purest example of Amiga hardware preservation shading into alternate history: not copying a Commodore board, but completing an enthusiast-imagined one.

entries.imageCredit: Hardware photo: AmiBay community listing
entries.name: ReAmiga 1200
entries.what: A redrawn, fabbable A1200 PCB that also fixes known Commodore bugs. The files are public and boards have been built worldwide since 2019.
entries.why: The basis for several commercial "new A1200" builds, and the project that made replica motherboards a normal part of the scene.

entries.name: ReAmiga 3000 / 4000 / A4000TX
entries.what: Replica and redrawn big-box boards: ReAmiga 3000 with battery and quirk fixes, community A4000 Rev B recreations, and the ATX-format A4000TX "Tesseract" remake.
entries.why: They extend replica manufacture to the big-box machines whose original boards are scarcest and most battery-damaged.

entries.name: A2000 replica
entries.what: An open-source KiCad recreation of the Amiga 2000 motherboard.
entries.why: It brings the replica approach to the machine that defined Amiga expandability.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: Apollo Computer / Exec.pl
entries.name: Vampire V4 Standalone
entries.what: A complete Amiga-compatible computer with no Commodore parts: the Apollo 68080 FPGA CPU, SAGA chipset generation 4 (Isabel video, Arne audio, Anni DMA) with up to 12 MB chip RAM and both AGA and RTG modes, 512 MB–1 GB DDR3, USB, dual DB9, 100 Mbit Ethernet and a 128 GB CF card preloaded with ApolloOS.
entries.why: The first new-built 68k Amiga-class computer of the modern era, and proof that the FPGA branch could go beyond recreation into extension.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected Apollo A6000 image — Gearnews
entries.name: Apollo A6000 "Unicorn"
entries.what: Apollo's flagship complete computer: an A600-inspired wedge with a mechanical Amiga-layout keyboard, 68080, full SAGA and RTG, 2 GB fast RAM, dual SD slots, a 128 GB CF card with ApolloOS, USB-C power and digital video out. Sold in limited batches.
entries.why: Arguably the first brand-new 68k Amiga-compatible with a built-in keyboard since 1994 — a new machine, not a restoration.

entries.name: Checkmate A1500 Plus
entries.what: A modern re-issue of the classic Checkmate A1500 case, accepting A500, A600, A1200, Mini-ITX and Micro-ATX boards via modular trays. A compact A1500 Mini variant and a hand-built 19-inch 4:3 IPS retro monitor with native 15 kHz support accompany it.
entries.why: It gives restored, emulated and next-gen Amiga builds a shared physical design language without sacrificing original cases.

entries.name: GVP accelerator families
entries.what: The largest US accelerator line: the A530 Turbo sidecar (68EC030 at 40 MHz with SCSI), G-Force 030/040 for the A2000, A1230 Turbo+ for the A1200 and the TekMagic 060.
entries.why: GVP defined the American Amiga upgrade market and the combo card — CPU, RAM and SCSI on one board.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Amiga Hardware Database
entries.name: phase5 Blizzard 12xx
entries.what: The definitive A1200 trapdoor accelerators: Blizzard 1230 I–IV, 1240T/ERC and 1260, with up to 256 MB and an optional SCSI Kit IV. The Blizzard 2060 served the A2000.
entries.why: The gold standard of classic acceleration, and still the boards modern designs are measured against. Several redrawn Blizzard PCBs circulate today.

entries.name: phase5 CyberStorm 040/060
entries.what: A3000/A4000 CPU-slot 68040 and 68060 boards — MK-I, MK-II and MK-III, the last adding Ultra-Wide SCSI.
entries.why: The big-box counterpart to the Blizzard line, and the platform the CyberStorm PPC later built on.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Amiga Hardware Database
entries.name: phase5 BlizzardPPC
entries.what: A dual-processor A1200 card placing a PowerPC 603e at 160–240 MHz alongside the existing 68040/68060, with a connector for the BVisionPPC graphics card.
entries.why: It created the installed base that AmigaOS 4 Classic and MorphOS 1.x would later target — and today it is among the most expensive classic Amiga hardware on the used market.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Amiga Hardware Database
entries.name: phase5 CyberStormPPC
entries.what: The A3000/A4000 equivalent: a PowerPC 604e at 150–233 MHz beside a 68040/68060, with Ultra-Wide SCSI and a CyberVisionPPC connector.
entries.why: The most powerful classic Amiga configuration of the era, and the only way besides emulation to run AmigaOS 4.1 Classic on a real big-box Amiga.

entries.name: Apollo / ACT accelerators
entries.what: The 1990s "Apollo" line — 1230/1240/1260, 2030, 3040/3060, 4040/4060 — offering budget alternatives to the Blizzards. Unrelated to today's Apollo Team.
entries.why: A frequent source of naming confusion in the modern scene, and a reminder how crowded the 1990s accelerator market was.

entries.name: M-Tec, DKB, CSA & others
entries.what: The rest of the crowded classic field: M-Tec 68020i and E-Matrix 530, DKB Cobra and Wildfire 060, CSA Derringer and Twelve Gauge, Harms Professional 3000, Microbotics VXL-30 and M1230XA, ICD AdSpeed, Supra SupraTurbo, Kupke Golem and DCE Typhoon.
entries.why: Represented as a family rather than individually — a literal accelerator encyclopedia would run to hundreds of SKUs.

entries.name: ACA 12xx family
entries.what: Individual Computers' A1200 trapdoor line: the ACA1234 (68030 at 25–50 MHz, 128 MB, MapROM), the flagship ACA1240 and ACA1260 (68040 or 68060 with 256 MB), plus the budget ACA1221lc and the ACA1211 RAM/IDE-speeder.
entries.why: The longest continuously produced modern accelerator family, and the commercial backbone of A1200 upgrading. Note: iComp stopped shipping to the USA in December 2025.

entries.name: ACA620 family
entries.what: Individual Computers' accelerator line for the Amiga 600, since discontinued.
entries.why: It briefly made the A600 a credible upgrade target before Vampire and PiStorm took that role.

entries.name: ACA500plus
entries.what: An A500 side-slot expansion: 68000 at 14/42 MHz, 8 MB fast RAM, dual CF slots for boot and auxiliary storage, a Kickstart flashing and menu system, and a slot to piggyback ACA12xx accelerators.
entries.why: The most complete single upgrade for an unexpanded A500 — CPU, RAM, storage and multiple Kickstarts in one board. In production since 2017.

entries.name: Furia EC020
entries.what: An A600 plug-over accelerator: 68EC020 at 33 or 40 MHz, up to 9.5 MB fast RAM and an optional FPU.
entries.why: The standard inexpensive A600 speed-up for over a decade, and still sold.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Epsilon's World
entries.name: Vampire V2 accelerators
entries.what: Cyclone III-class FPGA accelerators for the A600 (V600, 2016), A500 (V500, 2017) and A1200 (V1200, 2019), each with the Apollo 68080 core, 128 MB RAM, HDMI out and SAGA RTG.
entries.why: The boards that made the 68080 real and transformed what a classic Amiga could do. Officially end-of-support since October 2025, with core development frozen as the FPGA filled up.

entries.name: TerribleFire 5xx family
entries.what: Open-source Verilog 68030 boards plugging into the 68000 socket of the A500, A1000, A2000 and CDTV — the TF534 and the TF536 with integrated RAM and IDE.
entries.why: TerribleFire proved a hobbyist could open-source a competitive accelerator design and let anyone build it, reshaping the economics of the scene.

entries.name: TerribleFire 12xx family
entries.what: A1200 trapdoor accelerators: the TF1230 (68030) and the TF1260 (68060), the latter a closed design sold through authorised builders and one of the most popular modern 060 boards.
entries.why: It brought 68060 performance back into affordable reach for A1200 owners.

entries.name: TerribleFire 3xxx/4xxx & CD32
entries.what: Boards for the big boxes and console: the TF330/TF328 CD32 expansion-slot 68030 and RAM boards, the open CD32 riser adding IDE and experimental USB, and the TF4060 68060 CPU-slot board for the A4000.
entries.why: They made the CD32 upgradeable into a real computer, and gave A4000 owners a modern 060 option.

entries.name: Warp accelerator family
entries.what: High-end 68060 boards: the Warp 1260 for the A1200 (up to ~100 MHz, 256 MB, microSD, RTC, audio codec, FastIDE), plus Warp 560 for the A500 and Warp 4060 for the A3000/A4000.
entries.why: The fastest 68060 boards of their moment. The line now appears dormant — the product site redirects to CS-Lab's CNC business and no distributor lists them as of 2026.

entries.name: Wicher boards
entries.what: A Polish family covering nearly every machine: the Wicher 500i 68030 trapdoor accelerator, Wicher CD32 and CDTV boards, and the 508i, 608 and 1211 RAM/IDE expansions.
entries.why: It fills the gap between bare RAM expansions and full accelerators, especially for the CD32 and CDTV.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: Retro Ready
entries.name: PiStorm
entries.what: A 68000-socket adapter carrying a Raspberry Pi, for the A500, A500+, A1000 and A2000. With the default Musashi emulator it performs like a 100–125 MHz 68030; with Emu68 it far exceeds any real 68060. It also provides RTG via the Pi GPU, virtual SCSI, RAM and networking.
entries.why: Open source under MIT, it collapsed the cost of a fast Amiga from hundreds to tens — the single most disruptive hardware project of the 2020s.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: AmigaKit
entries.name: PiStorm32-Lite
entries.what: The A1200 trapdoor PiStorm for the Raspberry Pi 4 family — now the mainstream A1200 accelerator. A PiStorm16 variant serves the 16-bit-bus A600.
entries.why: It made an A1200 faster than any period hardware for the price of a game, and normalised the ARM-plus-real-chipset hybrid.

entries.name: Framethrower / FT600
entries.what: RGB-capture add-ons that pipe native chipset video into the Raspberry Pi so a single HDMI cable carries both native and RTG output.
entries.why: It solves the PiStorm's one real awkwardness — two video paths, two cables — and makes the hybrid feel like one machine.

entries.name: Apollo Firebird V4
entries.what: The V4-generation Cyclone V board for the Amiga 500, carrying the 68080 and SAGA into original A500 hardware.
entries.why: It brought the V4 architecture — and its much larger FPGA — to the best-selling Amiga.

entries.name: Apollo Icedrake V4
entries.what: The V4-generation board for the Amiga 1200.
entries.why: The most capable single upgrade available for an original A1200, and the V4 line's best seller.

entries.name: Apollo Manticore & Salamander V4
entries.what: V4-generation boards for the Amiga 600 (Manticore) and CD32 (Salamander).
entries.why: They completed the V4 line-up across nearly every classic machine.

entries.name: Apollo Phoenix V4
entries.what: Announced September 2024 for the Amiga 1000: 68080, SuperAGA, flicker-fixer, FastKick and Ethernet.
entries.why: The oldest Amiga finally got the newest CPU — closing the loop forty years after the A1000 shipped.

entries.name: Buffee
entries.what: A 68000-socket accelerator using a TI Sitara ARM running PJIT, a pipelined just-in-time translator, rather than a Raspberry Pi. In development since 2020 with no shipping product yet.
entries.why: The most credible alternative approach to PiStorm's architecture — a self-contained module rather than a carrier for someone else's SBC.

entries.name: A3660 & BFG9060
entries.what: Community remakes of 68060 CPU cards for the big boxes: the A3660 recreates the Commodore A3640-class card, and the BFG9060 is a community 68060 CPU-slot accelerator sold in small batches.
entries.why: They keep A3000 and A4000 CPU upgrades available now that original cards are scarce.

entries.name: The 68060 supply problem
entries.what: No 68060 has been manufactured since the 1990s. Every modern 060 board depends on recovered rev6 (71E41J) full-featured chips, which overclock past 100 MHz — while the grey market is full of re-marked EC/LC060 parts lacking MMU and FPU, sold as full 060s.
entries.why: A standing buyer warning for TF1260, Warp and ACA1260 purchases, and the structural reason FPGA and ARM alternatives took over.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Amiga Hardware Database
entries.name: Picasso II / IV
entries.what: The most common classic RTG cards. Picasso II/II+ used Cirrus Logic GD542x on Zorro II; the 1996 Picasso IV added Zorro II/III autosensing, an integrated flicker-fixer and module slots for the Pablo video encoder, Paloma TV tuner and Concierto sound.
entries.why: For many users the Picasso IV was the single card that turned an Amiga into a usable modern workstation.

entries.name: CyberVision 64 / 3D / PPC
entries.what: phase5's RTG line: CyberVision 64 (S3 Trio64), CyberVision 64/3D (S3 ViRGE with optional scandoubler and MPEG modules), and the Permedia 2-based CyberVisionPPC and BVisionPPC that attach only to the PPC accelerators.
entries.why: The cards that carried CyberGraphX, and the only 3D-capable option for PowerUP owners.

entries.name: Retina, Merlin, Piccolo & other RTG
entries.what: The wider classic RTG field: MacroSystem Retina Z2 and Retina BLT Z3 (and DraCo's Altais), X-Pert Merlin and Domino, Ingenieurbüro Helfrich Piccolo and Piccolo SD64, oMniBus, and GVP's EGS Spectrum.
entries.why: A crowded market that made retargetable graphics a normal expectation years before the PC world settled on one driver model.

entries.name: Mediator PCI & Prometheus
entries.what: PCI busboards for Zorro Amigas — Elbox Mediator (1200 TX and 4000D MK-III still sold) and Matay Prometheus — letting Voodoo 3/4/5, ViRGE and Radeon cards run as RTG under Picasso96. DCE's GRex did the same for PPC owners.
entries.why: They opened the vast, cheap PC graphics market to Amiga users, and enabled Warp3D-era 3D gaming.

entries.imageCredit: Hardware photo: Individual Computers
entries.name: Indivision ECS / AGA
entries.what: Internal flicker-fixers that tap the video chip socket: Indivision AGA MK3 for the A1200 and A4000 with VGA and digital output up to 1280×1024, and Indivision ECS V3 for OCS/ECS machines.
entries.why: The standard way to put a real Amiga on a modern monitor without RTG — no external box, no lag, native inside the case.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: MNT Research
entries.name: MNT ZZ9000
entries.what: An FPGA-plus-ARM Zorro II/III autosensing card: RTG to 1920×1080, gigabit Ethernet, USB, and an ARM coprocessor that can offload MP3 and video decoding. The ZZ9000AX adds 16/24-bit audio; a ZZ9000CX for native video capture is announced.
entries.why: The first genuinely new Zorro graphics card in twenty years, and the most capable — open hardware, still receiving firmware updates.

entries.name: RGBtoHDMI
entries.what: A Denise-socket digital tap plus Raspberry Pi Zero firmware giving pixel-perfect, zero-lag HDMI from any 12-bit-video Amiga, in internal and external builds.
entries.why: Open source and inexpensive, it delivers a cleaner picture than any analogue scandoubler by never converting to analogue at all.

entries.name: Scandoublers & external scalers
entries.what: The wider video-out field: ScanPlus ECS/AGA internal scandoublers, the external Medusa, generic OSSC and RetroTINK line-multipliers widely used on Amiga RGB SCART, and the open GBS-Control firmware for cheap GBS-8200 upscalers.
entries.why: Between them they cover every budget from £20 to £700 for the single most common modern Amiga problem: getting a picture.

entries.name: Toccata, Prelude & Delfina
entries.what: The classic 16-bit sound cards: MacroSystem's Toccata (Zorro II, 16-bit/48 kHz — the studio standard), ACT's Prelude and clockport Prelude 1200, and Petsoff's DSP56002-based Delfina and Delfina Lite.
entries.why: They lifted Amiga audio past Paula's 8-bit ceiling and were the reason AHI existed.

entries.name: Melody & MPEG audio cards
entries.what: Melody Z2 and Melody 1200: 16-bit cards with hardware MPEG audio decoding.
entries.why: Early proof that a 68k Amiga could play MP3 without the CPU doing the work — the idea Prisma Megamix later perfected.

entries.name: Prisma Megamix
entries.what: A clockport hardware audio decoder built on a VS1063-class codec, playing MP3, FLAC and more with almost no CPU load and mixing with Paula. Supports AHI and MHI.
entries.why: The poster child for the MHI standard: it lets a stock-speed A1200 act as a music player. Sold in repeated batches.

entries.name: MNT ZZ9000AX
entries.what: An audio expansion for the ZZ9000: 16/24-bit playback with an AHI driver, offloading MP3 decoding to the card's ARM resources.
entries.why: It completes the ZZ9000 as a single card handling graphics, network and sound.

entries.name: AmiGUS
entries.what: A new FPGA-based Zorro II sound card — streaming DAC plus wavetable, GUS-inspired — with AHI and MHI drivers, in first batches around 2025.
entries.why: Evidence that even the quietest corner of the hardware scene is still producing new designs.

entries.name: Classic SCSI controllers
entries.what: Commodore's A590 sidecar, A2091 and A4091 Zorro cards and A2090; GVP's HD8+ and Series II; and third-party boards from Supra, ICD, Microbotics HardFrame, Oktagon 2008 and Fastlane Z3.
entries.why: They gave the Amiga fast, standard mass storage a decade before IDE arrived on the A600.

entries.name: IDE-to-CF / SD adapters
entries.what: Commodity CF2IDE and SD2IDE adapters — plus 44-pin DOM SSDs and mSATA-to-IDE — are the default boot solution for the A600, A1200 and A4000.
entries.why: Solid-state, silent, instantly backed up by pulling the card: the single cheapest and most transformative classic upgrade.

entries.name: Elbox FastATA
entries.what: Four-device IDE speeders for the A1200 and A4000 with PIO-5 and UDMA modes, now in a CF/SATA Black Edition.
entries.why: It removes the crippling slowness of the stock Gayle IDE interface — still in production after 25 years.

entries.imageCredit: Product photo: My Retro Store
entries.name: Gotek + FlashFloppy
entries.what: A cheap USB-stick floppy emulator running Keir Fraser's open-source FlashFloppy firmware, sold pre-flashed by most Amiga dealers. OLED and rotary-encoder mods are common.
entries.why: It replaces the most failure-prone part of any Amiga with a £20 device, and lets ADF collections run on real hardware.

entries.name: HxC2001 floppy emulators
entries.what: The original floppy-emulator ecosystem — SD HxC, Slim SD, USB HxC — plus licensed HxC firmware for Gotek hardware and the Pauline forensic floppy tool. Actively maintained since 2006.
entries.why: It created the HFE format and the whole category Gotek later commoditised.

entries.name: SCSI2SD / ZuluSCSI / BlueSCSI
entries.what: SD-card SCSI drive and CD emulators for SCSI-equipped Amigas. The current ZuluSCSI Blaster (RP2350B) reaches 18 MB/s and can emulate a network adapter over Wi-Fi; open-source BlueSCSI v2 offers the same idea.
entries.why: They keep A590, A2091, A3000, A4091 and GVP systems running now that period SCSI drives are dying, and sneak Ethernet into machines that never had it.

entries.name: RIPPLE IDE & lide.device
entries.what: An open IDE stack: the RIPPLE Zorro II IDE controller for the A2000, A3000 and A4000 with autoboot from Kickstart 1.3, 2 TB support, ATAPI and CD boot — plus the open lide.device driver used by several community IDE cards.
entries.why: It finally gave the big boxes modern, large, bootable IDE storage, and removed even the 2 TB limit.

entries.name: Buddha IDE
entries.what: Zorro II IDE controllers: the original re-released in 2017 and the redesigned Buddha Plus One from 2023, still receiving firmware updates.
entries.why: The commercial, supported counterpart to RIPPLE for Zorro machines.

entries.name: SDBox & parallel-port storage
entries.what: A parallel-port SD-card reader with an spisd.device driver, for machines with no other expansion available.
entries.why: It gives even a completely unexpanded A500 a route to modern storage.

entries.name: X-Surf / X-Surf 100
entries.what: Zorro II/III autosensing 100 Mbit Ethernet cards, with an option to piggyback a RapidRoad USB module.
entries.why: The de-facto big-box network card, and still sold — the simplest way to get a classic Amiga online.

entries.name: plipbox
entries.what: An open-source Arduino parallel-port-to-Ethernet bridge for machines with no expansion slots.
entries.why: It puts the cheapest possible Amiga on a network using a £5 microcontroller.

entries.name: PCMCIA Ethernet & Wi-Fi
entries.what: CF-format and 16-bit NE2000 or 3Com cards on the A600 and A1200 via cnet.device, and Prism2/2.5 Wi-Fi cards driven by Neil Cafferkey's prism2.device — WPA supported, WPA2 limited. Dealers sell pre-configured cards.
entries.why: The only wireless option for stock A600 and A1200 machines, and the reason the PCMCIA slot still matters.

entries.name: RapidRoad USB
entries.what: High-speed USB for the A1200 clockport or as an X-Surf 100 piggyback, running the Poseidon stack.
entries.why: The most widely available modern USB option for classic Amigas.

entries.name: Deneb, Subway & Algor
entries.what: E3B's USB hardware: the Zorro II/III Deneb with USB 2.0 and flash ROM, the clockport Subway for the A1200, and the newer announced Algor. Produced in occasional small batches.
entries.why: Deneb remains the fastest USB option for Zorro machines, and the one that could boot from USB.

entries.name: A314
entries.what: A Raspberry Pi used as a *coprocessor* rather than a CPU replacement, in trapdoor (A500), A314-600, A314-1000 and clockport variants. A shared-RAM link provides file systems, networking, remote display and audio streaming.
entries.why: A genuinely different idea from PiStorm: keep the 68000 in charge and let the Pi be a service processor. Open source and still active.

entries.name: mouSTer
entries.what: A USB-to-DB9 adapter emulating Amiga and Atari mice, joysticks and wheel modes, with firmware updates. Project update posted June 2026.
entries.why: It lets a modern optical mouse work on an original Amiga — solving one of the worst daily-use annoyances.

entries.name: Tank mouse & controller remakes
entries.what: Injection-moulded remakes of the classic tank mouse (later wireless and optical versions), optical conversion kits for original mice, CD32-compatible pads, ArcadeR DB9 sticks — and a licensed TAC-2 reissue announced in August 2026.
entries.why: New-manufacture input devices mean the whole experience, not just the computer, can be restored.

entries.name: Keyrah & AmiKey
entries.what: Keyrah V3 turns original Amiga and C64 keyboards and joysticks into USB devices for PCs and emulation; AmigaKit's AmiKey does the reverse, attaching USB keyboards to original A600 and A1200 machines.
entries.why: Two halves of the same idea: the feel of original hardware, wherever the computing actually happens.

entries.name: The A1200 clockport
entries.what: A small, cheap internal expansion header intended for a real-time clock, which the community turned into a universal peripheral bus: RapidRoad, Subway, Prisma Megamix, Delfina Lite, Melody 1200, A314-cp — and four-way expanders when one is not enough.
entries.why: An accidental standard: the most-used expansion interface on the most-used Amiga, for a purpose Commodore never intended.

entries.name: DiagROM
entries.what: A ROM-based hardware diagnostic that boots on a machine too broken to run anything else, testing CPU, RAM, chipset and ports and reporting over serial. V2.0 was a major rewrite.
entries.why: The indispensable first tool of Amiga repair — free, and the reason thousands of dead boards were fixed rather than scrapped.

entries.name: Amiga Test Kit
entries.what: A disk-loadable test suite for memory, chipset, drives, ports and video, including CRT test cards.
entries.why: The companion to DiagROM for machines that do boot — the standard post-repair verification step.

entries.name: KickSmash32
entries.what: An open-source Kickstart flash module for the A1200, A3000, A4000 and A4000TX: eight switchable ROM banks, in-system flashing, and USB-C file services (smash and smashftp).
entries.why: It makes swapping Kickstart versions a menu choice, and doubles as a file-transfer route needing no network at all.

entries.name: MegAChip & chip-RAM expansion
entries.what: DKB's classic 2 MB chip-RAM board for the A500 and A2000, remade and sold for years by Individual Computers, plus LIV2's open adapter retrofitting a 2 MB Agnus into 1 MB boards.
entries.why: Chip RAM is the hardest classic limit to raise, and these are the only ways to raise it.

entries.name: ZorRAM & fast-memory boards
entries.what: Autoconfig fast RAM without a CPU upgrade: LIV2's open GottaGoFastRAM (8 MB for the A500, A1000, A2000 and CDTV), trapdoor boards like the A608mini and A1208 V3, ZRAM 8 and AmigaKit's ZORRAM, and iComp's 256 MB BigRamPlus for Zorro III.
entries.why: RAM is what most 68k software actually wants, and these deliver it far more cheaply than an accelerator.

entries.name: Custom-chip replacements
entries.what: Drop-in FPGA and CPLD re-implementations of Agnus, Denise, Paula and the 8520 CIA have all been demonstrated — leveraging the open Minimig cores — but none is in volume production as of 2026. Gary substitutes exist; Gayle, Akiko, Ramsey and Super Buster rev 11 have no replacements at all, so repairers still rely on donor boards.
entries.why: The one remaining gap in Amiga sustainability: every other part can now be remade, but the custom chips are still finite.

entries.name: Recapping & battery removal
entries.what: Every A600, A1200, A4000, CD32 and CDTV needs surface-mount recapping, and every A500+, A2000, A3000 and A4000 needs its Varta or barrel battery removed before it destroys the board. Polymer and MLCC kits are stocked by all major dealers.
entries.why: Repair item number one, and the single most common reason a stored Amiga no longer works. Treated by the community as mandatory maintenance, not restoration.

entries.name: New cases & keyboards
entries.what: New injection-moulded A1200 cases in several colours including translucent, new A500 cases, A600 tooling in polling, plus a new mechanical Amiga keyboard with a modular expansion bay and fresh keycap sets in many national layouts.
entries.why: It closes the loop on complete new-build Amigas: with a ReAmiga board, a new case, a new keyboard and a modern PSU, nothing in the machine need be 30 years old except the custom chips.

entries.name: Modern power supplies
entries.what: Modern high-efficiency replacements with correct connectors: iComp's CA-PSU, Keelog's newly manufactured square bricks, Polish-made units, and DIY builds around Mean Well modules using open PCBs.
entries.why: Original 30-year-old bricks are considered board-killers when their regulation drifts. Replacing the PSU is the cheapest insurance an Amiga owner can buy.

entries.name: File-transfer bridges
entries.what: Ways to move files without a network: Cloanto's Amiga Explorer over null-modem serial or TCP, plain null-modem with Term or NComm, Greaseweazle and Gotek sneakernet, PCMCIA CF cards, and KickSmash32's USB-C file services.
entries.why: The unglamorous problem every returning Amiga owner hits first, and the half-dozen answers the community settled on.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Tduk (Alex Lozupone), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: AmigaOS / Workbench 1.x
entries.what: The launch operating system: pre-emptive multitasking with a windowing GUI on 256 KB, built partly on the TRIPOS heritage in BCPL. 1.3 (1988) added the FastFileSystem with hard-disk autobooting and the recoverable RAM disk.
entries.why: It did in 1985 what mainstream desktop systems would not manage for years. The blue-and-orange palette was chosen for contrast on a television set.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amiga UNIX (AMIX) — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga UNIX (AMIX)
entries.what: Commodore's full AT&T System V Release 4 port for the A2500UX and A3000UX, with X11 and Open Look.
entries.why: One of the earliest commercial SVR4 ports anywhere — killed by workstation pricing, thin application support and Commodore's decline.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Greg Donner's Workbench archive
entries.name: AmigaOS 2.x
entries.what: A complete visual and architectural modernisation debuting with the A3000: the 3D-look GUI, the GadTools and BOOPSI widget frameworks, public screens, Commodities, the Installer, and AmigaDOS rewritten from BCPL into C. 2.1 added Locale, AmigaGuide and CrossDOS.
entries.why: It established the API surface that every later Amiga-like system — AmigaOS 4, MorphOS, AROS — still implements.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Chiffre01, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: AmigaOS 3.0 / 3.1
entries.what: Shipped with the AGA machines: datatypes (system-wide file-format plugins), localised Workbench and CD-ROM foundations. 3.1 (1994) was Commodore's last release and was re-issued by Amiga Technologies in 1996.
entries.why: For nearly 25 years, 3.1 *was* the compatibility standard — the baseline every 68k application, game and pack assumed.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Linux/m68k on Amiga — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Linux/m68k on Amiga
entries.what: Linux on 68k Amigas: an official Debian release architecture from 2.0 (1998) through 3.1 (2005), dropped from official Debian with 4.0, and still alive as an unofficial debian-ports architecture with modern kernels.
entries.why: It still works — on accelerated, PiStorm or emulated machines — making the Amiga one of the longest-supported Linux platforms ever.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for NetBSD/amiga — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: NetBSD/amiga
entries.what: A maintained tier-2 port running on any Amiga with a 68020 or better and an MMU, including the 68060 and DraCo. A minimal NetBSD/amigappc also exists.
entries.why: Still receiving current releases in 2026 — the most actively maintained Unix for classic Amiga hardware. OpenBSD's Amiga port died in 2002.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AROS project (SourceForge)
entries.name: AROS Research Operating System
entries.what: An open-source re-implementation of the AmigaOS 3.1 APIs — like Wine rather than an emulator — running native on bare hardware or hosted under Linux, Windows and macOS, with the Wanderer desktop and the Zune MUI clone. Licensed under the AROS Public License.
entries.why: The only Amiga-like system that is free, open and multi-architecture. Activity is high: roughly 2,000 commits a year, IPv6, USB 3, an AArch64 Raspberry Pi port, and a RISC-V port with stable nightlies from August 2026.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for pOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: pOS
entries.what: A portable, API-compatible AmigaOS clone shipped as a 68k beta with demo applications, with PowerPC and x86 ports planned. Abandoned by about 1998.
entries.why: The first attempt at what AROS eventually achieved — and a casualty of the post-Commodore market collapse.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for PowerUP / WarpOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: PowerUP / WarpOS
entries.what: The two rival PowerPC kernels for phase5's dual-processor cards: phase5's PowerUP (ppc.library, Ralph Schmidt) and Haage & Partner's WarpUP/WarpOS (Sam Jordan) — incompatible executable formats and context-switching schemes competing on the same boards.
entries.why: The "PPC kernel war" split a tiny market. WarpOS won most commercial games; PowerUP's lineage led directly to MorphOS, whose ABox still runs both formats today.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmigaOS 3.5 — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmigaOS 3.5
entries.what: A software-only update requiring a 68020, 3.1 ROMs and a hard disk. It added the ReAction GUI toolkit, the GlowIcons set, support for hard disks over 4 GB, a CD filesystem and bundled internet software.
entries.why: The first sign that AmigaOS development could continue commercially after Commodore — and the release that introduced ReAction, still the official toolkit today.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amiga DE / Amiga Anywhere — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amiga DE / Amiga Anywhere
entries.what: Amiga Inc.'s "digital environment" built on Tao Group's intent and Elate portable VM: write once, translate binaries at install time to any CPU. An SDK and a player with small commercial games appeared for Windows and PocketPC.
entries.why: It had no connection to real AmigaOS code, and evaporated when Tao Group collapsed in 2007 — the clearest example of the brand being pointed away from its own technology.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmigaOS 3.9 — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmigaOS 3.9
entries.what: Added AmiDock, unified archive handling via XAD, a file finder, a media player and an improved Shell, followed by two official "BoingBag" update packs.
entries.why: The end of the Haage & Partner line and, for eighteen years, the most advanced classic AmigaOS available. Still the base of many community distributions.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: operating-system.org
entries.name: MorphOS 1.x
entries.what: Begun in 1999 by Ralph Schmidt and colleagues from the phase5 world, first running on PowerUP accelerator cards and then bundled with the Pegasos. Architecture: the proprietary Quark microkernel supervising the ABox, a PPC-native AmigaOS API clone binary-compatible with 68k applications via the Trance JIT and with both PowerUP and WarpOS executables.
entries.why: It made the "blue" PowerPC branch real, and its ABox remains the most compatible Amiga runtime ever built.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amithlon — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amithlon
entries.what: An audacious "AmigaOS on x86": a stripped Linux kernel booting straight into a highly optimised JIT 68k emulator running an almost unmodified AmigaOS 3.9. On period Athlons it was by far the fastest Amiga ever sold.
entries.why: It proved the AmigaOS experience was separable from 68k silicon years before anyone else managed it — then died in a three-way licensing dispute in 2002–03.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmigaOS XL / AmigaXL — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmigaOS XL / AmigaXL
entries.what: The other half of the AmigaOS XL box: AmigaOS 3.9 running hosted on QNX 6 on x86, using QNX for hardware drivers.
entries.why: Technically interesting, commercially stillborn — and a reminder that Amiga Inc. had itself announced QNX as the next-generation foundation in 1998.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AmiGANG
entries.name: AmigaOS 4.0
entries.what: The PowerPC-native continuation of the official line, developed under Hyperion's 2001 contract with Amiga Inc. It introduced the ExecSG kernel — licensed from its authors, the Frieden brothers — and the Petunia JIT that runs 68k applications at native speed.
entries.why: The first genuinely new official AmigaOS in a decade, and the release that made "AmigaOS" a living product name again.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AROS 68k — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AROS 68k
entries.what: A from-source 68k build of AROS providing a free, redistributable replacement Kickstart ROM and Workbench for real Amigas, emulators and FPGA cores.
entries.why: The only legal no-licence route to a booting Amiga — which is why UAE, MiSTer, Vampire and PiStorm setups all ship it as their default fallback. Compatibility is good but not equal to a real Kickstart.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for MorphOS 2.x — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: MorphOS 2.x
entries.what: The commercial standalone release, adding Efika support and a native TCP/IP stack — and then, from 2.4 onward, the celebrated second life on Apple hardware beginning with the Mac mini G4 and eMac.
entries.why: Supporting used Macs was the decision that saved MorphOS: cheap, plentiful, repairable hardware for a system whose purpose-built boards were rare.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: MorphOS team, GPL (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: MorphOS 3.x
entries.what: The long 3.x line: PowerBook G4 and many more PPC Macs, then in 3.10 (2018) the AmigaOne X5000 and ACube Sam460, followed by steady modernisation through 3.11–3.19.
entries.why: It turned MorphOS into the most polished Amiga-like desktop in daily use, with genuinely modern applications — above all the Wayfarer browser.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AmigaOS.net
entries.name: AmigaOS 4.1 Final Edition
entries.what: The mature AmigaOS 4 line: hardware-compositing GUI, JXFS, memory paging, a unified graphics library and support for over 2 GB of RAM. Update 2 (2020) touched 200+ components; Update 3 (October 2025) brought 60+ new features, ~70 updated components, 135+ fixes, 4K display support and a new USB stack. A refreshed SDK followed in June 2026.
entries.why: The official AmigaOS as it stands today, on Classic PPC, AmigaOne, Pegasos II, Sam and X5000 hardware, the A1222 Plus, and under QEMU. AmigaOS 4.2 is announced but unreleased.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Greg Donner's Workbench archive
entries.name: AmigaOS 3.1.4
entries.what: The revival of classic 68k development after 24 years — forked from 3.1 rather than 3.9 for licensing reasons. Support for the whole 680x0 line to the 68060, large hard disks including at boot, a modernised Workbench, and crucially new physical Kickstart ROMs.
entries.why: It proved there was still a paying market for classic AmigaOS, and it put newly manufactured Kickstart chips back on dealers' shelves.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ApolloOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ApolloOS
entries.what: A fork of AROS 68k optimised for the Apollo 68080 and SAGA chipset, with AMMX acceleration, USB and Ethernet support. Ships preinstalled on the CF cards supplied with V4 hardware.
entries.why: It gives Vampire and A6000 owners a complete, legal, no-licence-required system out of the box — the answer to the ROM problem that dogged earlier Vampire boards.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AmigaOS 3.2 / TechSpot
entries.name: AmigaOS 3.2
entries.what: Over 100 new features: integrated ReAction, Workbench management of ADF images, a context-sensitive Help system, improved datatypes, a better Shell and Kickstart 3.2 (V47) ROMs for every model. Point releases ran to 3.2.3 in April 2025, with updates free to registered owners; digital download since March 2026.
entries.why: The current classic AmigaOS, and the most capable 68k system ever released. AmigaOS 3.3 is in development — but Hyperion's 68k licence expires at the end of 2027, after which stewardship passes to Amiga Corporation.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Charlie / AmigaSpirit
entries.name: MorphOS 3.20
entries.what: The current MorphOS: support for the new Mirari T1042 platform with dedicated drivers and thermal management, expanded Radeon support with better HDMI/DVI/DisplayPort handling, the SFS2 filesystem (files over 4 GB, partitions to 2 TB), Ambient improvements and new bundled tools. A matching SDK with GCC 15.2 shipped alongside.
entries.why: A fully functional free demo that merely slows after 30 minutes has made MorphOS the easiest next-gen system to actually try. Supporting brand-new hardware in 2026 signals continued PowerPC commitment; an x86-64 port remains discussed but unreleased.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Emu68 project documentation
entries.name: Emu68
entries.what: A bare-metal 68040-plus-FPU JIT translator for ARM. A Raspberry Pi on a PiStorm board boots directly into a translated 68k environment running real AmigaOS 3.x with no Linux underneath — with 4-way JIT caching, PiStorm16 support and early PowerPC translation work.
entries.why: Effectively the fastest 68k Amiga ever made, and the software half of PiStorm's disruption. It also exposes the Pi's Wi-Fi to AmigaOS as a SANA-II device.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for FriendOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: FriendOS
entries.what: A browser-based "cloud OS" from an Amiga-scene veteran, open-sourced as FriendUP. The commercial operation appears defunct, though the repositories remain.
entries.why: The best-known AmigaOS-*inspired* system that is not an Amiga system at all.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: CCOM / Christian Corti
entries.name: AmigaDOS
entries.what: The DOS layer — filesystems, processes, the command set — derived from MetaComCo's TRIPOS and originally written in BCPL. Its BPTR oddities survived until AmigaOS 2.0 rewrote DOS in C; OS 4.0 finally dropped the BCPL legacy.
entries.why: Assigns, logical device names, and pluggable handlers like RAM:, CON: and PIPE: gave the Amiga a filesystem model that still feels modern.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for CLI / AmigaShell — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: CLI / AmigaShell
entries.what: The command-line environment — CLI in 1.x, renamed AmigaShell from 2.0 — with its own console handler, scripting, redirection and full multitasking.
entries.why: The substrate every shell replacement extends or replaces, and the reason serious Amiga work was never confined to icons.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Greg Donner
entries.name: Workbench
entries.what: The desktop and graphical file manager, presenting disks, drawers and tools as icons backed by .info files — scriptable, extensible and famously lean. It can display multiple draggable screens at different resolutions and depths simultaneously.
entries.why: The interface the whole platform is remembered by. From AmigaOS 3.5 onward "AmigaOS" names the system and "Workbench" only the desktop.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for WShell — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: WShell
entries.what: A commercial replacement shell from the author of ARexx and ConMan: command history, aliases, filename completion, scripting conveniences and a better console.
entries.why: The Amiga's open console and process design encouraged Unix-like shell experimentation remarkably early — WShell in 1988 predates most of what PC users had.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ConMan — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ConMan
entries.what: A replacement console handler for AmigaDOS 1.2 and later, adding line editing, command history and function-key recall to the bare native console.
entries.why: Console handling was left thin in the shipped system, and third-party handlers like this one set the expectations that KingCON and ViNCEd were later built to meet.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: ScummBlog
entries.name: Directory Opus 4
entries.what: The classic lister-based dual-pane file manager whose configurable buttons and filetypes became the power-user standard. GPSoftware released the source under the GPL in 2000, enabling community builds and a MorphOS port.
entries.why: So central to Amiga workflow that opening the source kept it alive for another twenty-five years.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ZShell — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ZShell
entries.what: A compact third-party shell known for command-line editing, history and a very small memory footprint. Unrelated to Unix zsh.
entries.why: It exemplifies the many lightweight userland replacements distributed through Aminet and the disk-magazine scene.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ViNCEd — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ViNCEd
entries.what: A full vi-like console and shell replacement with tab expansion, review buffers and extensive editing — and the default console of AmigaOS 3.9. Still actively maintained after 34 years.
entries.why: One of the longest continuously developed pieces of Amiga software in existence.

entries.imageCredit: Release graphic: MorphOS team
entries.name: Magic User Interface (MUI)
entries.what: The object-oriented GUI toolkit that became the dominant third-party framework on classic Amiga and the *native* toolkit of MorphOS — font-adaptive, user-configurable layouts with per-application preferences.
entries.why: MUI let users restyle every application at once, decades before theming was normal. Most serious modern Amiga software is a MUI application.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for MagicWB, NewIcons & GlowIcons — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: MagicWB, NewIcons & GlowIcons
entries.by: Martin Huttenloher, Nicola Salmoria, Matt Chaput
entries.what: The three icon aesthetics that defined the Amiga desktop: Huttenloher's 8-colour MagicWB grey 3D look (1993–96), Salmoria's palette-independent NewIcons, and Chaput's 256-colour two-state GlowIcons introduced with AmigaOS 3.5 and still stock today.
entries.why: MagicWB in particular is the visual base every modern enhancement pack still emulates — an aesthetic set by a shareware author, not a vendor.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for KingCON — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: KingCON
entries.what: A drop-in CON: and RAW: console replacement with filename tab-completion, a review buffer and menus.
entries.why: Thirty years on it is still bundled by nearly every enhancement pack — a two-decade-old binary that nobody has needed to replace.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for MCP, MultiCX & the patch culture — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: MCP, MultiCX & the patch culture
entries.what: The commodity and system-patch tradition: MCP (Master Control Program) bundling dozens of patches at once, MultiCX (re-released as giftware in March 2025), MagicMenu (revived to v3.1 in August 2026), ToolsDaemon, ToolManager, FBlit and FText for chip-RAM relief, and BlazeWCP for faster planar Workbench.
entries.why: A whole culture of tiny, surgical system modifications — the reason two Amigas running the same OS version can feel completely different.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ClassAct / ReAction — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ClassAct / ReAction
entries.by: Phantom Development, then Haage & Partner / Hyperion
entries.what: A free BOOPSI class collection that competed with MUI, adopted by Haage & Partner as ReAction for AmigaOS 3.5 and now the official toolkit of both AmigaOS 4.x and AmigaOS 3.2.
entries.why: The official answer to MUI — and the reason modern AmigaOS has a consistent native look without licensing a third-party toolkit.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Directory Opus Resource Centre community
entries.name: Directory Opus Magellan
entries.what: DOpus 5's radical follow-up, which can *fully replace Workbench*: its listers and desktop take over icons, menus and the desktop itself. Open-sourced under the AROS Public License in December 2012 and ported by the dopus5allamigas project to AmigaOS 3, AmigaOS 4, MorphOS and AROS.
entries.why: The most complete Workbench replacement ever built, and the default desktop of AmiKit and an option in Icaros.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for amiwm — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: amiwm
entries.what: A stacking window manager for the X Window System that reproduces the Workbench interface — screens, drawers and window gadgets — on Unix and Linux desktops. Source-available rather than free software: unmodified source may be redistributed for non-commercial purposes only.
entries.why: Treats the Workbench idiom as something portable in its own right, independent of both the chipset and the OS, and has kept it running on X11 for a quarter of a century.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Scalos — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Scalos
entries.what: The best-known dedicated Workbench *replacement*: a reimplementation with multithreading, plugins, true-colour icons and MUI-based preferences, for 68k, AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS. Open source, now dormant.
entries.why: It showed the desktop itself was replaceable component software, not part of the OS — still widely installed despite years without a release.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmiStart — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmiStart
entries.what: A configurable start-menu, taskbar and dock bringing familiar menu conventions to classic Workbench and Amiga-like desktops.
entries.why: A common ingredient in curated distributions, and often the first thing that makes Workbench feel navigable to a newcomer.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Ambient — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Ambient
entries.what: MorphOS's integrated MUI-based desktop, GPL-opened in 2005 and maintained as part of the OS ever since.
entries.why: It proves an Amiga-like desktop could be rebuilt from scratch and end up feeling more modern than the original, not merely different.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Wanderer — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Wanderer
entries.what: AROS's bundled Workbench clone, built on Zune and shipped with every AROS distribution.
entries.why: The free-software Workbench — the piece that lets AROS feel like an Amiga rather than merely implement its APIs.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Zune — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Zune
entries.what: AROS's open-source reimplementation of the MUI API, and the basis of Wanderer.
