entries.why: It let the enormous body of MUI software concepts move into a fully free system.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Arcade Game Selector (AGS/AGS2) — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Arcade Game Selector (AGS/AGS2)
entries.what: A minimal joystick-driven fullscreen menu that boots straight into a game list with screenshots, with OCS and AGA layouts and background image loading.
entries.why: The launcher that made a real Amiga behave like a console — and the foundation of both AmigaVision's front end and HstWB's game packages.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for iGame — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: iGame
entries.what: The most popular on-Amiga WHDLoad front end: a MUI application that scans repositories for slaves and shows screenshots, genres and metadata, with builds for AmigaOS 3, AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS.
entries.why: The polished, Workbench-native way to browse a few thousand games — and still actively developed.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for X-bEnCh — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: X-bEnCh
entries.what: A WHDLoad launcher and more: it auto-scans drives for slaves and executables, manages manuals, and includes a mini file manager and CLI, with 128-colour OCS/ECS and 272-colour AGA interfaces.
entries.why: Designed to run on any 68k Amiga, it made curated collections usable on unexpanded machines.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for TinyLauncher — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: TinyLauncher
entries.what: An ultra-light WHDLoad, demo and module front end with retro styling, joystick and keyboard control, cover art, an integrated mod player and even MiSTer vadjust support.
entries.why: Built for stock 68000 machines where iGame and MUI are too heavy — and updated more often than almost anything else in this category.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmiBench — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmiBench
entries.what: AmigaKit's proprietary desktop environment, shipped as the installed system on the A600GS and A1200NG. It is built on the company’s System Release V46 — a modified AROS with an AROS Kickstart replacement ROM — supplemented by further AROS components. Copyright notices run from 2018; it reached buyers with the A600GS in June 2024.
entries.why: The appliance route taken to its conclusion: an AROS-derived Workbench pre-installed on low-cost ARM hardware, so the buyer meets a finished desktop instead of assembling one from an OS, an emulator and a disk image.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected official Amiga Forever screenshot
entries.name: Amiga Forever
entries.what: The official preservation and emulation suite: preconfigured WinUAE and WinFellow with *licensed* Kickstart ROMs and OS versions, RP9 game packages, prebuilt Workbench environments, galleries and video. The Plus edition covers every ROM and OS from 0.7 to 3.X; companion Essentials apps supply licensed ROMs on Android.
entries.why: The one legal, one-click route into Amiga emulation — and the ROM source most other emulators and packs point users toward.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ClassicWB — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ClassicWB
entries.what: The reference "instant retro Workbench": menu-driven theming across MagicWB, NewIcons and GlowIcons, sensible patches, tools and a WHDLoad-ready structure — in LITE, FULL, ADV, ADVSP, P96 (RTG), UAE, OS3x and minimal 68K editions.
entries.why: For twenty years the default answer to "how do I set up a nice Workbench?" — complete rather than abandoned, and still installable automatically through HstWB.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmigaSYS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmigaSYS
entries.what: A Hungarian preconfigured Workbench pack, popular around 2005–2010 as the main AmiKit alternative for WinUAE, E-UAE and real AGA machines. Discontinued; the original site is gone.
entries.why: One of the two packs that established the whole "preconfigured Amiga desktop" genre.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AmiKit
entries.name: AmiKit
entries.what: The flagship modern retro desktop: over 400 applications on a full OS 3.x environment with the DOpus Magellan desktop, MUI 5, antialiased TrueType fonts, dark mode, high-resolution RTG screens, LiveUpdate — and the signature Rabbit Hole, which launches host Windows, macOS and Linux applications from inside the Amiga desktop. X13 adds start-menu styles, a Mini Launcher and KIT, an AI assistant built on AmigaGPT.
entries.why: The most polished Amiga desktop anyone has assembled, on Windows, macOS, Linux, Raspberry Pi, USB stick, Vampire and PiStorm. It requires your own AmigaOS and Kickstart files.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Icaros Desktop — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Icaros Desktop
entries.what: The flagship AROS x86 (ABIv0) desktop distribution: a full live-and-install system with AmiBridge 68k integration via Janus-UAE, optional DOpus Magellan desktop, media tools and a large software collection.
entries.why: For over a decade the easiest way to actually *use* AROS. A November 2025 post — "Until we meet again, Icaros Desktop" — effectively mothballed the project, pointing users to the AROS World community.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AROS Broadway — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AROS Broadway
entries.what: An early AROS x86 distribution aimed at a media-friendly desktop. Defunct; last preview 2016.
entries.why: Part of the first wave of attempts to package AROS for ordinary users.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AspireOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AspireOS
entries.what: A lightweight AROS distribution aimed at Acer Aspire One netbooks. Dead — the domain is parked.
entries.why: It made AROS run genuinely well on real, cheap, portable hardware.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AEROS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AEROS
entries.what: A hybrid AROS-on-Linux distribution for x86 and Raspberry Pi, once sold with AresOne PCs. Dormant — the domain now redirects elsewhere.
entries.why: It pioneered the pragmatic hybrid model — Linux underneath for drivers, AROS on top for the experience — that AxRuntime later formalised.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for BetterWB / BestWB — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: BetterWB / BestWB
entries.what: Lightweight enhancement packs that work on a plain 68000 with 2 MB: curated fixes, handlers and small upgrades without the bulk of the big packs. BetterWB targets AmigaOS 3.1, BestWB targets 3.1.4.
entries.why: The choice for people who want a *better* stock Workbench rather than a different one — and the only serious option for unexpanded machines.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AfA OS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AfA OS
entries.what: A daring enhancement layer grafting AROS 68k components onto AmigaOS 3.1 and 3.9: an RTG-friendly Workbench, antialiased TrueType text, larger icons and a faster GUI.
entries.why: It moved code *from* the open clone *into* the proprietary original — the reverse of the usual direction, and a neat illustration of how blurred the boundaries are.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Amibian — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Amibian
entries.what: A Raspberry Pi image designed to boot in seconds straight into an Amiga emulator and present itself as a dedicated appliance — initially UAE4ARM-based, later Amiberry.
entries.why: It made "turn a Pi into an Amiga" a reproducible path for non-experts, and set the template Pimiga and the Pi editions of AmiKit followed. (The similarly named Amibian.js is an unrelated browser-based project.)

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for CoffinOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: CoffinOS
entries.what: A performance- and visuals-focused community distribution of a customised AmigaOS 3.x/3.9 environment, strongly associated with Vampire and heavily accelerated machines: large preinstalled software collections, RTG and SAGA-tuned Workbench, games and emulators out of the box.
entries.why: It demonstrates the appetite for opinionated "super Amiga" systems — and it is the standing example of why legal sourcing matters, since builds bundle copyrighted material and hardware vendors publicly distance themselves from it.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for CaffeineOS — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: CaffeineOS
entries.what: A curated, performance-focused 68k environment likewise associated with Vampire hardware.
entries.why: One of several community attempts to package SAGA and 68080 capabilities into a coherent desktop.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Flower Pot — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Flower Pot
entries.what: A guided Windows installer that automated building an AmigaOS 4.1-under-emulation environment — WinUAE with the PowerPC plugin preconfigured — while deliberately requiring the user's own purchased 4.1 ISO.
entries.why: It lowered the barrier to trying AmigaOS 4 without scarce PowerPC hardware. Its page has since vanished and the project appears dead.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AROS One — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AROS One
entries.what: Now the most active AROS distribution family, with editions for x86 32-bit ABIv0, 64-bit ABIv11 tracking deadwood's builds, and a 68k edition for real Amigas and emulators.
entries.why: With Icaros mothballed, AROS One is where the AROS desktop scene has consolidated.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for ApolloOS system image — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: ApolloOS system image
entries.what: The ready-to-run ApolloOS card image shipped with V4 hardware and distributed for download — a complete AROS 68k desktop tuned for the 68080, with software preinstalled.
entries.why: The legal, vendor-supported alternative to community Vampire images: nothing copyrighted, nothing to source yourself.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Mercury Vapour
entries.name: PiMIGA
entries.what: A popular Raspberry Pi and x86 "instant Amiga" image: Amiberry-based with a full desktop and large WHDLoad libraries, distributed free by torrent. The author and community stress that it should never be paid for.
entries.why: The most widely used turnkey Amiga image — and a legal grey zone, since builds have historically included Kickstart, OS and game material, which is why mainstream Amiga archives do not host it.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AmigaVision
entries.name: AmigaVision
entries.what: Formerly MegaAGS: roughly 5,300 hand-tuned game and demo configurations with per-title chipset, CPU and scaling settings, high-resolution screenshots and metadata, integer overscale, dynamic PAL/NTSC pixel aspect, curated lists, 2,955 QR-coded manuals, WHDLoad-based saving and PFS. Open-source build tooling; you supply the software.
entries.why: The most rigorous preservation-minded environment in the scene, and the only one that targets MiSTer, Analogue Pocket, Raspberry Pi, desktop emulators *and* real A1200, A4000 and CD32 hardware from one build.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for HstWB Installer — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: HstWB Installer
entries.what: An automated image builder: point it at your own AmigaOS files (3.1 through 3.2 or 3.9, identified by checksum) and Kickstarts, and it builds ready HDF or directory setups with optional ClassicWB, BetterWB, EAB WHDLoad packs, iGame, AGS2 and its own launcher.
entries.why: It turns "assemble a perfect Amiga install" from a weekend of manual work into a scripted, repeatable build — MIT-licensed and legally careful by design.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Chrysalis — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Chrysalis
entries.what: A one-installer software pack for MorphOS adding curated applications, games, emulators, Ambient configuration, codecs and skins to a fresh installation.
entries.why: The MorphOS equivalent of AmiKit: it turns a clean install into a fully equipped desktop in one step.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Enhancer Software — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Enhancer Software
entries.what: A commercial component and application pack for AmigaOS 4.1: RadeonHD and RadeonRX drivers, Warp3D Nova, updated datatypes and commands, and applications like MultiViewer, MultiEdit and X-Dock. A free Enhancer Core line is distributed via the AmiSphere platform.
entries.why: Effectively a second system layered on AmigaOS 4 — and the centre of a long-running dispute with Hyperion over duplicated components and the ExecSG kernel.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Wwwwolf, GPL (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: UAE
entries.what: The ancestor of virtually all Amiga emulation, first released in 1995 and originally named the "Unusable Amiga Emulator" because at first it could show only a white screen. Later re-expanded to Unix, then Universal Amiga Emulator. GPL.
entries.why: It established the 68000-plus-OCS emulation model every descendant still carries, and made the Amiga one of the best-preserved platforms in computing.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Fellow / WinFellow — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Fellow / WinFellow
entries.what: The historic non-UAE alternative: Fellow began as a DOS Amiga emulator famed for speed, and WinFellow is its Windows port focused on OCS and ECS gaming. Dormant since around 2019–21, though Amiga Forever still bundles a build.
entries.why: For years it was the fast option when UAE was too slow — and proof that more than one codebase could do the job.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Reindersweb / WinUAE
entries.name: WinUAE
entries.what: The reference Amiga emulator and effectively the R&D lab for the whole ecosystem: cycle-exact OCS/ECS/AGA, 68000–68060 with MMU and FPU, JIT, PowerPC accelerator emulation, CD32 and CDTV with Akiko, Toccata, x86 bridgeboards, dozens of expansion boards, Picasso96 RTG, and a debugger regarded as the best for 68k anywhere. Version 6.0.0 (2025) rewrote the Agnus/Alice and Denise/Lisa emulation almost completely.
entries.why: The accuracy benchmark every other implementation, including FPGA cores, is measured against. GPL, Windows x86 only.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for MAME Amiga systems — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: MAME Amiga systems
entries.what: MAME's amiga.cpp driver covers the A500, A1000, A2000, A3000, A1200 and CD32, plus the Amiga-based arcade platforms Arcadia Systems, Cubo CD32 and Upscope. The computer drivers are flagged preliminary; the arcade ones are more usable.
entries.why: It brings Amiga hardware into the single largest systematic preservation project in computing — and preserves the arcade machines nothing else covers.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for E-UAE — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: E-UAE
entries.what: "Enhanced UAE": a merge of the stagnant UAE 0.8.x Unix trunk with WinUAE features, notably the JIT, for Linux, macOS, BeOS and AmigaOS hosts. Last release 2007.
entries.why: Genealogically crucial — nearly every later portable fork, from PUAE to Janus-UAE, built on it.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for UAE4All / UAE4ALL2 — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: UAE4All / UAE4ALL2
entries.what: The speed-over-accuracy fork family, originally targeting the Dreamcast and GP2X and based on a very early UAE.
entries.why: It put the Amiga on handheld hardware a decade before that was normal, and started the mobile lineage that ends at Amiberry.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Janus-UAE — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Janus-UAE
entries.what: An E-UAE fork for AROS, notable for "coherency mode": 68k Amiga applications integrated directly into the AROS desktop rather than confined to an emulator window.
entries.why: It is the engine behind Icaros's AmiBridge, letting an open-source Amiga-like system run the entire classic software library seamlessly.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: FS-UAE project
entries.name: FS-UAE
entries.what: A cross-platform emulator wrapping the WinUAE core in a portable SDL/OpenGL shell with a polished fullscreen UI, per-game configuration and — uniquely in the UAE world — built-in netplay. Its Launcher identifies disk images by checksum against the OpenRetro database and auto-configures everything.
entries.why: The best "it just works" desktop Amiga emulator on macOS and Linux, and the deterministic netplay engine behind AmigaLive.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for PUAE / libretro core — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: PUAE / libretro core
entries.what: The Amiga core of RetroArch and most console-style distributions. Despite keeping the PUAE name it has been progressively rebased onto WinUAE sources (currently 5.3.1): A500 through A4000, CD32 and CDTV, every common disk format, WHDLoad .lha direct launch, M3U multi-disk, run-ahead — and a built-in AROS ROM for instant starts.
entries.why: It is how most people accidentally run an Amiga: inside RetroArch, on a phone, a console, a handheld or a TV box.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Scripted Amiga Emulator — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Scripted Amiga Emulator
entries.what: A pure JavaScript and HTML5 re-implementation of UAE and WinUAE code running entirely in the browser, covering OCS and ECS configurations. Dormant.
entries.why: Historically important far beyond its activity level: the Internet Archive's in-browser Amiga software library runs on it through the Emularity loader.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for UAE4ARM — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: UAE4ARM
entries.what: The ARM JIT fork with Picasso96 support that was *the* Raspberry Pi and Pandora Amiga emulator before Amiberry superseded it.
entries.why: It made the £35 computer a credible Amiga, and directly seeded both Amibian and Amiberry.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected Amiberry artwork — BlitterStudio
entries.name: Amiberry
entries.what: The dominant Amiga emulator outside Windows: WinUAE-grade compatibility plus features WinUAE lacks, above all WHDLoad auto-boot — drop an .lha on it and it builds the whole boot environment automatically. Runs on Linux (ARM, x86-64, RISC-V), macOS including Apple Silicon, Windows, Android with a native touch UI and Android TV, FreeBSD and Haiku. v8.0 moved to SDL3 and a new ImGui interface.
entries.why: The engine hidden inside a remarkable amount of consumer hardware and turnkey imagery — Pimiga, Amibian, AmiKit for Pi, and reportedly the retail mini-consoles.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for Denise — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: Denise
entries.what: A cycle-accurate multi-system emulator covering the C64 and the Amiga 500, 1000 and 600, with run-ahead (rare in Amiga emulation), CRT shaders, rewind, floppy audio and a debugger. Windows, macOS, Linux and BSD.
entries.why: One of only two active from-scratch alternatives to the UAE lineage, and the only one offering run-ahead latency reduction.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for QEMU AmigaNG targets — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: QEMU AmigaNG targets
entries.what: Mainline QEMU now emulates the PowerPC machines AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS run on: Sam460ex (from QEMU 3.0), Pegasos2 (6.1), the dedicated amigaone machine (8.2) and mac99 PowerMacs. QEMU 11.0.0 (April 2026) improved ati-vga so the AmigaOS 4.1 Radeon driver works.
entries.why: It makes the next-generation systems genuinely testable without rare, expensive PowerPC hardware. AmigaOS 4.1 installs and runs on all three machines, easiest via the BBoot loader; MorphOS runs on Pegasos2 and mac99.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for AmigaLive — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: AmigaLive
entries.what: A netplay lobby application for synchronised multiplayer of classic Amiga games, with game lobbies, a Discord community and organised tournaments. Built on FS-UAE's deterministic netplay — not WinUAE, contrary to common belief.
entries.why: It restored something the Amiga barely had in period: reliable, organised online multiplayer for a 1990s games library.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for vAmiga — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: vAmiga
entries.what: A from-scratch cycle-accurate emulator of the Amiga 500, 1000 and 2000 (OCS and ECS) with a beautiful native macOS interface, run-ahead and an extensive inspector and debugger suite, plus the RetroVault companion for disk tooling.
entries.why: The most approachable accurate emulator on the Mac, and the codebase behind vAmigaWeb.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for vAmigaWeb — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: vAmigaWeb
entries.what: A WebAssembly port of the vAmiga core, installable as a progressive web app with touch controls — currently the most practical route to an Amiga on an iPhone or iPad.
entries.why: It puts a cycle-accurate Amiga one URL away, with nothing to install and no app store to satisfy.

entries.imageCredit: Curated source for qemu-uae (PPC plugin) — see images/catalog-completion/SOURCES.md
entries.name: qemu-uae (PPC plugin)
entries.what: Not an emulator but the crucial plugin: a stripped QEMU PowerPC 603e/604e core packaged so that both WinUAE and FS-UAE can emulate BlizzardPPC and CyberStormPPC accelerator CPUs.
entries.why: It is what allows an emulated A1200 or A4000 to boot AmigaOS 4.1 Classic — the bridge between the classic and next-generation branches.

entries.imageCredit: Photo: Amiga Hardware Database
entries.name: RTG — Retargetable Graphics
entries.what: The concept that made a classic Amiga usable on a modern monitor: a driver layer between graphics.library and the hardware, so Workbench and applications render in high-resolution chunky modes on graphics cards, FPGA cores or virtual emulated boards instead of directly through OCS, ECS or AGA planar modes.
entries.why: The single most important modernisation of the platform. It is also why "AmigaOS-compatible" does not imply custom-chip compatibility: DraCo, AmigaOne, Sam and X5000 machines rely on RTG and system APIs rather than recreating a chipset.

entries.name: CyberGraphX
entries.what: One of the two historic RTG systems, tied to phase5's CyberVision cards, which introduced the CGX API that many applications and games still call. No longer developed standalone — but MorphOS's graphics subsystem is its direct descendant.
entries.why: It popularised retargetable screens first, and its author became a MorphOS core developer, carrying the design forward.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Emu68 P96 setup documentation
entries.name: P96 (Picasso96)
entries.what: The de-facto RTG standard on classic Amigas: a modular driver system supporting Cirrus, S3, Voodoo, Matrox, Permedia2, CyberVision, Picasso IV, ZZ9000, Vampire SAGA and the UAE virtual card. Freeware originally, bought and commercially maintained by iComp since 2017, with Hyperion co-owning the PowerPC branch.
entries.why: It won the classic market by offering a cleaner driver model, emulating its rival's API, and staying free — and it is still actively gaining support for hardware built in the 2020s.

entries.name: Warp3D
entries.what: The original Amiga 3D driver API for ViRGE, Permedia2 and Voodoo cards — fixed-function, and still the target of many classic games.
entries.why: It gave the Amiga hardware-accelerated 3D at the same moment the PC world was standardising on OpenGL and Direct3D.

entries.name: Warp3D Nova & ogles2
entries.what: The modern shader-based 3D stack for AmigaOS 4: Warp3D Nova (GLSL-style shaders and vertex buffers) with Daniel Müßener's ogles2.library implementing OpenGL ES 2.0 on top, plus GL4ES bringing desktop OpenGL to that.
entries.why: The workhorse behind modern AmigaOS 4 game ports — it is what let Quake 2 and Irrlicht-based software arrive on the platform in 2024.

entries.name: TinyGL & MiniGL
entries.what: The OpenGL implementations of the next-generation systems: MorphOS's built-in TinyGL, substantially rewritten by Mark Olsen and further updated in MorphOS 3.20, and AmigaOS 4's older MiniGL subset layered on classic Warp3D.
entries.why: They are why cross-platform 3D software can be ported to these systems at all.

entries.name: Wazp3D
entries.what: A software, CPU-only implementation of the Warp3D API, letting classic Warp3D games run with no 3D card at all. A Vampire fork drives the SAGA and Maggie hardware.
entries.why: It rescued a whole generation of 3D games for users who never owned the specific cards they required.

entries.name: SAGA chipset
entries.what: The FPGA chipset accompanying the Apollo 68080: video (Isabel), audio (Arne), DMA (Anni), up to 12 MB chip RAM, 16 large sprites, AGA-compatible modes plus SuperAGA extensions, RTG over HDMI, and the Maggie 3D unit.
entries.why: The most consequential *revisionist* project in the scene: rather than only reproducing Commodore silicon, it extends it — which is why "compatible" now spans faithful recreation through deliberate augmentation.

entries.name: AMMX & the Apollo 68080
entries.what: A superscalar 68k-compatible FPGA CPU with 64-bit extensions and the AMMX SIMD instruction set, claiming performance well beyond any real 68060. The core is closed source.
entries.why: It divides the community: unsanctioned ISA extensions draw fragmentation criticism, and the closed core draws objections from the open-FPGA world — but it is also the only project actively growing the 68k architecture rather than preserving it.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: AmigaOS Documentation Wiki
entries.name: AHI — Audio Hardware Interface
entries.what: The retargetable audio standard: applications open ahi.device and audio routes to Paula or to any sound card through driver plug-ins. The classic 68k standard remains v4.18; the v6 rewrite is what AmigaOS 4, MorphOS and AROS integrate.
entries.why: RTG's counterpart for sound — and the reason a single application can address Paula, a Toccata, a Prisma Megamix or a ZZ9000AX without knowing anything about them.

entries.name: MHI — MPEG Hardware Interface
entries.what: A small standard API for hardware MPEG and MP3 decoders, so a 68k Amiga can play compressed audio with near-zero CPU load. Still in use: mhimasplayer for MAS-Player dongles, and MASWaver (2026) streaming web radio to MHI hardware.
entries.why: The pragmatic answer to Paula's limits — offload rather than emulate.

entries.name: bsdsocket.library
entries.what: The Amiga's de-facto socket ABI: every TCP/IP stack exports the same BSD-style shared library, so any network application runs on any stack.
entries.why: A community-established standard, not a vendor one — and the reason thirty years of Amiga internet software still works on current systems.

entries.name: AmiTCP & Genesis
entries.what: The original 1993 stack that defined bsdsocket, later commercialised, with its lineage continuing in Genesis — the stack bundled with AmigaOS 3.5 and 3.9.
entries.why: It put the Amiga on the internet before most home computers had any TCP/IP at all.

entries.name: Miami / MiamiDX
entries.what: The user-friendly commercial stacks of the late 1990s. Registration servers are long gone and development is dead, but installations are still encountered.
entries.why: For many users Miami was how the Amiga got online — a GUI over TCP/IP when the alternative was configuration files.

entries.name: Roadshow
entries.what: The modern commercial TCP/IP stack for 68k (OS 2.04 and later): fast, SANA-II, with a built-in firewall, DHCP and shell diagnostics, sold with a time-limited demo. AmigaOS 4's built-in stack is Roadshow-based and was updated again in Update 3.
entries.why: The current answer for classic networking, and the stack the official OS itself adopted.

entries.name: AmiSSL
entries.what: The shared OpenSSL port that every Amiga internet application depends on, released several times a year across 68k, AmigaOS 4, MorphOS and AROS.
entries.why: Without it the modern web would simply be unreachable from any Amiga. Keeping a 68k TLS stack current with upstream OpenSSL is one of the least glamorous and most essential jobs in the scene.

entries.name: Poseidon USB stack
entries.what: The USB stack for classic hardware — with Trident as its preferences GUI — supporting HID, mass storage, audio, network and printer classes across Deneb, RapidRoad, Subway and Algor hardware. Sources were opened, forming the basis of the AROS port; MorphOS bundles an integrated version and ApolloOS uses it for V4 USB.
entries.why: One person's stack became the platform standard, and then the shared foundation of three other operating systems.

entries.name: Sirion & ANAIS
entries.what: AmigaOS 4's own USB stack, Sirion, notably improved in Update 3 (October 2025) and joined by a USB Audio Class driver in August 2026 — plus ANAIS, a newer stack developed by AmigaKit for its Enhancer ecosystem.
entries.why: Two competing USB stacks on one OS is a neat illustration of the parallel AmigaOS 4 development ecosystems.

entries.name: PFS3 / PFS3-AIO
entries.by: originally Michiel Pelt, rebuilt by Toni Wilen
entries.what: The Professional File System III, open-sourced and rebuilt by Toni Wilen as a single "all-in-one" binary working from OS 1.x to 3.x on any 68000 or better, with TD64, NSD and SCSI-direct support and large partitions — much faster and far more crash-resistant than FFS.
entries.why: The community standard filesystem: AmigaVision, HstWB and most modern CF installs use it by default.

entries.name: SFS / SFS2
entries.what: SmartFilesystem, with safer write behaviour, popular on AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS. Its 64-bit SFS2 variant gained first-class support in MorphOS 3.20, handling files over 4 GB and partitions to 2 TB.
entries.why: The next-generation systems' native filesystem answer to FFS's limits.

entries.name: filesysbox.library
entries.what: A FUSE-compatible filesystem layer that lets Linux FUSE filesystems run as Amiga handlers — the enabler behind exFAT, NTFS-3G and smb2fs on 68k, AmigaOS 4 and AROS.
entries.why: A single clever abstraction that suddenly gave the Amiga access to every modern filesystem, without porting each one from scratch.

entries.name: FAT95, exFAT & NTFS support
entries.by: Torsten Jäger, Fredrik Wikström, Tobias Karlsson
entries.what: The stack that lets an Amiga read modern media: Torsten Jäger's free FAT95 for FAT12/16/32, exFAT-aos3 ported from the AmigaOS 4 implementation, and NTFS-3G with full read/write via filesysbox.
entries.why: It means a card written on a PC or Mac just works — the mundane compatibility that makes daily use practical.

entries.name: smbfs & smb2fs
entries.what: SMB filesystem clients: Olaf Barthel's classic smbfs, whose 2.x rewrite added SMB2 support, and Wikström's newer smb2fs built on filesysbox and libsmb2.
entries.why: The practical route to cloud storage on an Amiga — mount a NAS share and let something else sync it.

entries.name: IBrowse
entries.what: The long-lived native MUI browser for AmigaOS 3.0 through 3.2, AmigaOS 4.1 and MorphOS. Version 3.0a added OpenSSL 3 and TLS 1.3 via AmiSSL, better JavaScript and tabs. Its engine remains HTML 4.01-era.
entries.why: Thirty years of continuous commercial development by one person — and still the browser most classic Amiga users reach for.

entries.name: AWeb & Voyager
entries.what: The other two classic browsers: AWeb II, later open-sourced after being bundled with AmigaOS 3.5, and VaporWare's Voyager. Both dormant.
entries.why: Three competing native browsers on a platform this size says a lot about 1990s Amiga optimism.

entries.name: Odyssey Web Browser
entries.by: Fabien Coeurjoly, AROS build by deadwood
entries.what: A WebKit browser for MorphOS, the platform's mainstay until Wayfarer, with its final MorphOS release in 2015. It was ported to AmigaOS 4 and to AROS, where deadwood still maintains and modernises it.
entries.why: The first genuinely modern rendering engine on any Amiga-like system — and still the standard browser on AROS.

entries.name: NetSurf
entries.by: NetSurf project, Amiga port by Chris Young
entries.what: A small open-source engine with real CSS support, with AmigaOS 4 builds and 68k AGA and RTG builds.
entries.why: The pragmatic middle ground: modern enough CSS to render many current sites, light enough to run on a 68k machine.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: MorphOS Library
entries.name: Wayfarer
entries.what: A WebKit browser for MorphOS tracking an up-to-date WebKitGTK tree, with a JIT and WebAssembly support — described as the only current big-endian 32-bit PowerPC browser anywhere.
entries.why: The single most impressive piece of modern Amiga-family software: it makes a twenty-year-old PowerPC Mac a genuinely usable machine for the current web, and it is the strongest practical argument for MorphOS.

entries.name: AmiFox
entries.what: A 68k browser that offloads rendering to a server-side headless Chrome and streams the result back as images with clickable regions.
entries.why: A sideways solution to an impossible problem: the modern web on an unexpanded A500, by not rendering it locally at all.

entries.name: AmiTube & BoingTube
entries.what: YouTube clients for classic Amigas: AmiTube searches and downloads via a conversion server that transcodes to CDXL or MPEG, updated through February 2026, joined by the newer BoingTube in January 2026.
entries.why: Server-side transcoding is the same trick as AmiFox, applied to video — and it works on stock hardware.

entries.name: AmigaGPT
entries.what: A native ChatGPT client for AmigaOS 3.1 and later, AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS, with chat, image generation, speech output and support for custom OpenAI-compatible servers.
entries.why: A 1985 architecture talking to a 2026 language model over TLS — and now embedded in AmiKit X13 as its built-in assistant.

entries.name: YAM & SimpleMail
entries.what: The classic open-source MUI mail clients: YAM (Yet Another Mailer) with POP3, SMTP, TLS, PGP and filters, still producing 2.10 nightly builds, and the lighter SimpleMail. Both run on 68k, AmigaOS 4, MorphOS and AROS.
entries.why: Thirty years of continuous free-software email on a platform with no commercial incentive to bother.

entries.name: Iris
entries.what: A modern MorphOS mail client with real IMAP, OAuth2 for Gmail and Office 365, and HTML mail rendered through WebKit.
entries.why: OAuth2 support means MorphOS users can still reach mainstream mail providers that have locked out older clients.

entries.name: AmigaAMP
entries.what: The Amiga's WinAmp: MP3 and FLAC playback with skins, AHI output, MHI hardware offload, and Shoutcast and Icecast streaming with recording, for 68k and AmigaOS 4.
entries.why: Still updated in 2026 — twenty-eight years of releases, and the main reason a classic Amiga can be a music player.

entries.name: vbcc
entries.what: A portable ISO-C compiler suite and the reference for OS-friendly 68k C, targeting AmigaOS 1.2 through 3.x, Kickstart 1.x, AmigaOS 4, MorphOS, WarpOS and more.
entries.why: The compiler that keeps producing binaries that run on a stock 1985 machine — a discipline modern toolchains rarely maintain.

entries.name: vasm / vlink
entries.what: A retargetable assembler supporting Devpac and Motorola syntaxes across M68k, PowerPC, Z80 and 6502, with the matching vlink linker.
entries.why: The assembler of choice for the demoscene and modern game development — and half the reason cross-development from a PC became practical.

entries.name: ASM-One, AsmPro & Devpac
entries.what: The native on-Amiga assemblers of the 1990s — integrated editor, assembler, debugger and monitor in one program. AsmPro survives as freeware on Aminet.
entries.why: Generations of demos and games were written entirely inside these, on the machine itself, with no cross-compiler in sight.

entries.name: Bebbo's amiga-gcc
entries.what: A GCC-for-AmigaOS toolchain, defaulting to GCC 6.5.0 with extensive m68k optimisation work and experimental GCC 13.x branches.
entries.why: The standard "modern C on 68k" toolchain, and the foundation nearly every current Amiga C project builds on.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Bartman/Abyss, GPL-3.0
entries.name: amiga-debug (VS Code)
entries.what: A one-click VS Code extension that builds C and C++ with a bundled GCC 15.2, launches a bundled WinUAE or FS-UAE, and provides full source-level debugging, a cycle-accurate profiler, Copper and Blitter visualisers and size-profiled Shrinkler output.
entries.why: The tool that transformed modern Amiga development: the platform now has better debugging and profiling than it ever did commercially.

entries.name: Amiga Assembly (VS Code)
entries.what: A VS Code extension for 68k assembly with vasm and vlink integration, WinUAE and FS-UAE debugging, and documentation hovers.
entries.why: It brought modern editor tooling — completion, hovers, breakpoints — to hand-written 68k assembly.

entries.name: AmiBlitz 3
entries.what: An open-source (Apache-2.0) continuation of Blitz Basic 2 with a modern IDE, FPU support and updated includes.
entries.why: It keeps alive the BASIC dialect that produced a remarkable share of 1990s Amiga games, and it still gets releases.

entries.imageCredit: User-selected AMOS Professional screenshot — classicamiga.com
entries.name: AMOS & AOZ Studio
entries.what: AMOS Professional, whose source was released by its author, who now builds AOZ Studio — a transpiling modern AMOS targeting web and PC. New AMOS games still appear.
entries.why: AMOS taught a generation to program games, and its author is still working on the idea thirty-five years later.

entries.name: Hollywood
entries.what: A cross-platform multimedia and application language: one codebase compiles to 68k AmigaOS, AmigaOS 4, MorphOS, AROS, WarpOS, Windows, macOS, Linux, Android APKs and iOS, with an extensive plugin system and the Hollywood Designer visual tool.
entries.why: It inverts the usual relationship — an Amiga-native language that exports to modern platforms — and is the most commercially sustained Amiga development product still selling.

entries.name: REDPILL
entries.what: A free visual game creator that runs *on the Amiga itself*, covering OCS and AGA with sprites, tilemaps and simple physics — no cross-development required.
entries.why: Extremely active, and responsible for a large share of new freeware Amiga games: it lets people make games on the machine they love without learning assembly.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Mixel's Lab
entries.name: Scorpion Engine
entries.what: A free (closed-source) game engine and Windows IDE targeting the Amiga from an A500 upward, plus the Mega Drive and Neo Geo, from a single project.
entries.why: Behind a very large share of modern commercial Amiga releases — Metro Siege, Creeping Me Out and many others. Arguably the most productive single tool in the current scene.

entries.name: ACE (Amiga C Engine)
entries.what: An open-source (MPL-2.0) C framework for bare-metal Amiga game development, abstracting the Blitter and Copper while staying Kickstart 1.3-compatible.
entries.why: The middle path between assembly and an engine: modern C structure with direct hardware performance.

entries.name: dread engine
entries.what: The famous "Doom on an A500" rendering technology, first shown in the 2021 Dread demos and now driving the game GRIND. Public demo builds continue; a full release is still pending.
entries.why: It overturned a thirty-year assumption that texture-mapped first-person 3D was impossible on a stock 68000 Amiga.

entries.name: amitools / xdftool
entries.what: A Python toolbox that is the glue of modern Amiga build pipelines: xdftool for ADF and HDF images, rdbtool, romtool, hunktool, and vamos, which runs AmigaOS CLI binaries directly on a host machine.
entries.why: vamos in particular lets continuous-integration systems run genuine Amiga compilers with no emulator GUI at all.

entries.name: LLVM/Clang m68k backend
entries.what: The M68k backend has been in the LLVM tree since version 13 and keeps improving, but remains officially experimental — usable for bare-metal experiments rather than production AmigaOS work. Rust and Zig on 68k depend on it and are proof-of-concept only.
entries.why: If it matures, it is the route by which modern languages finally reach a 1979 CPU.

entries.name: SDKs & developer documentation
entries.what: The official kits: the free NDK 3.2 for classic AmigaOS, the AmigaOS 4.1 SDK refreshed in June 2026, the MorphOS 3.20 SDK with GCC 15.2 and Python 3.14, and AROS development via nightly contribs, deadwood's ABIv11 and AxRuntime. The ROM Kernel Reference Manuals remain readable online at amigadev.elowar.com.
entries.why: The Amiga is unusually well documented for its age — the original Commodore autodocs and RKMs are still the primary reference thirty years later.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Insert Disk 2
entries.name: WHDLoad
entries.what: The AmigaOS-friendly hard-disk install system for floppy-only games and demos: it loads them into an OS-clean environment, patches quirks — Kickstart dependencies, timing bugs, disk protection — adds trainers and quit keys, and returns cleanly to Workbench. New and updated installs are published continuously.
entries.why: The single most important classic-Amiga preservation project on real hardware. Nearly every launcher, pack and turnkey image in this atlas is built on it.

entries.imageCredit: KryoFlux photo: Gareth Halfacree, CC BY-SA 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Software Preservation Society (SPS/CAPS)
entries.what: Founded to preserve floppy software bit-perfectly, SPS created the IPF format — flux-derived images that include copy protection — and the CAPSimg library that lets WinUAE, FS-UAE, Amiberry and MAME read them. The site is online but visibly dormant.
entries.why: It set the standard for authentic disk preservation. Its restrictive licensing is also why GPL emulators must load CAPSimg as a separate user-downloaded plugin.

entries.name: KryoFlux
entries.what: SPS's own USB forensic floppy controller, sampling magnetic flux transitions; a de-facto standard at universities, museums and archives, with separate personal and institutional licensing.
entries.why: It professionalised disk archiving — and its non-commercial licensing terms are a large part of why fully open alternatives gained momentum.

entries.imageCredit: Hardware photo: Keir Fraser / Greaseweazle project
entries.name: Greaseweazle
entries.what: A fully open-source (Unlicense) USB flux reader and writer, with boards from around £10–£30 and support for nearly any floppy format.
entries.why: The community favourite of the 2020s: it made archiving your own disk collection cheap enough that thousands of people actually did it.

entries.name: DrawBridge / FloppyBridge
entries.what: An Arduino-based board and software to read and write ADFs and flux from real Amiga disks — whose killer feature, FloppyBridge, mounts a *real floppy drive* live inside WinUAE and Amiberry, with DrawBridge, Greaseweazle and SuperCard Pro all supported as bridges.
entries.why: It closes the loop between physical media and emulation: put a 1989 disk in a drive and it appears in a modern emulator.

entries.name: SuperCard Pro, FluxEngine & Applesauce
entries.by: Jim Drew / David Given / John Morris
entries.what: The rest of the flux-imaging field: Jim Drew's SuperCard Pro, origin of the widely supported .scp format; David Given's ~$15 MIT-licensed FluxEngine, which can also drive Greaseweazle hardware; and Applesauce, historically Apple-focused but now supporting Amiga DD and HD disks with AmigaDOS browsing and ADF export.
entries.why: Between them, flux-level archiving is now available at every price point from $15 to institutional.

entries.imageCredit: Historical screenshot: Aminet
entries.name: Aminet
entries.what: The historic centre of Amiga software distribution and long claimed as the largest public archive for any single platform of its era — still taking new uploads daily across 68k, PowerPC, MorphOS and AROS, with worldwide mirrors.
entries.why: Thirty-four years of continuous operation. Aminet is why so much Amiga software simply still exists, and why paths like `util/wb/` function as citations in this scene.

entries.name: OS4Depot, MorphOS Storage & AROS Archives
entries.what: The next-generation equivalents of Aminet: OS4Depot with over 4,500 files, MorphOS Storage with nearly 2,000 and more than a million downloads, and the slower-moving AROS Archives.
entries.why: Each living system maintains its own well-curated repository — a small ecosystem's version of a package manager.

entries.imageCredit: Archived site capture: Hall of Light / abime.net
entries.name: Hall of Light
entries.what: The definitive Amiga games database: releases, versions, credits, box, manual and media scans and screenshots, cross-linked with the Amiga Magazine Rack's reviews. Now served at amiga.abime.net behind anti-scraper protection.
entries.why: The reference catalogue of what was actually published on the Amiga — indispensable to preservation and to every launcher's metadata.

entries.name: Lemon Amiga & OpenRetro
entries.what: Lemon Amiga is a polished games database and community with roughly 4,500 titles, reviews and votes; OpenRetro is Frode Solheim's open, wiki-style *configuration* database — correct model, chipset, controls and WHDLoad variants — consumed live by the FS-UAE Launcher.
entries.why: OpenRetro in particular solved a specific problem: not what a game *is*, but exactly how to run it correctly.

entries.name: Amiga Magazine Rack
entries.what: An index of over 100 Amiga magazines with tens of thousands of scanned pages, every review and preview cross-linked to Hall of Light entries. Complete runs of Amiga Format, CU Amiga, Amiga World, Amazing Computing and Amiga Power are also mirrored on the Internet Archive.
entries.why: It preserves the *discourse* around the platform, not just its software — the reviews, the culture, the arguments.

entries.name: TOSEC
entries.what: A cataloguing project publishing DAT files that name and verify over 1,033,000 software sets across 300+ platforms, with the Commodore Amiga branch among the largest.
entries.why: It provides the canonical naming and checksums that make large collections verifiable rather than merely large.

entries.name: EAB File Server & Retroplay packs
entries.what: The English Amiga Board community file server: the canonical Retroplay WHDLoad game and demo packs — continuing Killergorilla's earlier work — plus OS packs, TOSEC sets and magazine scans, with free registration.
entries.why: This is where nearly every curated collection actually gets its content. AmigaVision, HstWB, iGame and AGS2 all assume it.

entries.name: Demozoo & Pouët
entries.what: The demoscene's primary databases: Demozoo with 188,851 productions, 135,461 music entries, 28,930 groups and 5,532 parties, edited daily and open source, and Pouët with 102,680 productions and over a million comments.
entries.why: Between them they document the Amiga's most distinctive cultural output more thoroughly than any commercial catalogue documents its software.

entries.name: ExoticA, Modland & Kestra BitWorld
entries.what: The music and scene archives: ExoticA and UnExoticA hold Amiga game and demo music in original native formats organised by game and composer; Modland is an enormous tracker-module archive across every format, updated to August 2026; and Kestra BitWorld is the deepest Amiga-specific scene index anywhere.
entries.why: They preserve formats no commercial player supports, playable via UADE's emulation of the original music routines.

entries.name: amigapcb.org & hardware databases
entries.what: Hardware-side preservation: the interactive layer-by-layer Amiga PCB Explorer for repair work, the Amiga Hardware Database (updated August 2026) documenting expansion cards with photos, autoconfig IDs and install disks, the Big Book of Amiga Hardware with 1,993 products, and AmigaWiki's schematics and service manuals.
entries.why: Board-level repair is only possible because someone documented the boards. These sites are why a 1992 A1200 can be traced and fixed in 2026.

entries.name: Internet Archive Amiga collections
entries.what: Large ADF, WHDLoad and TOSEC mirrors, complete magazine runs, and the Software Library: Amiga with titles playable directly in a browser through the Emularity loader and the Scripted Amiga Emulator.
entries.why: It brings Amiga software into the world's largest general-purpose archive, and makes it playable without installing anything.

entries.imageCredit: Logo: English Amiga Board
entries.name: English Amiga Board (EAB)
entries.what: The central English-language classic-Amiga forum and the hub of the preservation scene — WHDLoad development, Retroplay packs, Hall of Light and Magazine Rack coordination, hardware repair and coding — now behind anti-bot protection.
entries.why: If one place had to be called the home of the modern Amiga community, this is it.

entries.name: amiga-news.de
entries.what: Daily Amiga news in both German and English since 1998, with a complete archive back to that year and multiple items a day in 2026.
entries.why: The record of note for the whole ecosystem — the closest thing the scene has to a newspaper of record, and the primary source for much of this atlas.

entries.name: AmigaWorld, Amigans, MorphZone & a1k
entries.what: The system-specific communities: AmigaWorld.net and Amigans.net for AmigaOS 4, MorphZone (now at morph.zone) for MorphOS, AROS World for AROS, and the huge German-language a1k.org for hardware, repair and trading. Amiga.org, once among the oldest, is now effectively moribund.
entries.why: The next-generation branches each maintain their own centre of gravity — which is part of why the ecosystem reads as several communities rather than one.

entries.name: National communities
entries.by: PPA.pl, Amiga Impact, Obligement, Amigatronics, AmigaPage
entries.what: Poland's PPA.pl with daily news and a marketplace, France's Amiga Impact and David Brunet's monumental Obligement magazine with thousands of articles, Spain's Amigatronics, and Italy's AmigaPage.it.
entries.why: Poland in particular sustains an outsized share of modern Amiga hardware and game development — the scene is far more European and multilingual than English-language sources suggest.

entries.name: Print magazines in 2026
entries.what: Amiga still has newsstand print: Amiga Future (bimonthly since 1998, separate German and English editions, issue #182 in August 2026), Amiga Addict (UK, glossy, reached its 40th issue), Passione Amiga (Italy, #32 July 2026), Komoda & Amiga Plus (Poland, #30 July 2026), Boing (France, #11 June 2026) and Fusion Retro Books' ZZAP! AMIGA revival.
entries.why: Six or more current print magazines for a computer discontinued in 1994 is, by itself, the strongest evidence of what this atlas describes.

entries.name: The historic magazines
entries.what: The print culture that built the platform: Amiga Format (the UK giant), CU Amiga, the beloved iconoclast Amiga Power, Amiga World and Amazing Computing in the US, Germany's Amiga Joker — revived as a one-off special at Amiga40 in 2025 — The One, Amiga Action and Amiga Computing.
entries.why: Amiga magazine writing was unusually opinionated and literate, and its coverdisks were a distribution channel in their own right. All indexed at the Amiga Magazine Rack.

entries.name: Podcasts, YouTube & streaming
entries.what: Amigos Retro Gaming, The Retro Hour, 10 Minute Amiga Retro Cast, Dan Wood, GadgetUK164 for repairs, RMC – The Cave, Chris Edwards Restoration, Bill Winters' Amiga Bill Twitch show, Epsilon's Amiga Blog for next-gen systems — and Retro Recipes, whose host Christian "Perifractic" Simpson led the 2025 Commodore acquisition and now runs the company.
entries.why: Video became the platform's main outreach channel, and in at least one case the audience built there turned into ownership of the brand itself.

entries.name: Documentaries & books
entries.what: Jimmy Maher's The Future Was Here (MIT Press, 2012) on why the Amiga mattered technically; Brian Bagnall's Commodore: The Amiga Years (2017); David Pleasance's Commodore: The Inside Story (2018) and, with Trevor Dickinson, the three-volume From Vultures to Vampires on the post-Commodore IP saga; plus the documentaries Viva Amiga (2017), From Bedrooms to Billions: The Amiga Years (2016) and The Commodore Story (2018).
entries.why: The Amiga is unusually well served by serious history — including a university-press platform study, which few home computers can claim.

entries.name: Amiga37 / 38 / 39 / 40
entries.what: The Mönchengladbach event series that became the scene's centre of gravity: Amiga37 in October 2022 drew thousands and an all-star Commodore guest list, followed by Amiga38, Amiga39, and the 40th-anniversary Amiga40 in October 2025 — where the A1200NG was shown working and APC&TCP released the Amiga Joker revival special and two new games.
entries.why: It demonstrated that the community could fill a venue on the scale of a real trade show, twenty-eight years after the platform died commercially.

entries.name: AmiWest
entries.what: North America's premier Amiga show, held annually in Sacramento with A-EON as a longstanding sponsor, and traditionally where next-generation announcements and AmigaOS betas are shown.
entries.why: The AmigaOS 3.3 beta was first shown publicly at AmiWest in November 2025 — the show still functions as a genuine launch venue.

entries.name: Demoparties: Revision, Gerp & others
entries.what: Where new Amiga demos actually premiere: Revision at Easter in Saarbrücken — the world's biggest pure demoparty, with dedicated Amiga competitions, 2026 edition 3–6 April — plus Sweden's Amiga-heavy Gerp in January, Assembly, Evoke, and grassroots events like AmiParty and Amiga Rave-Craze.
entries.why: Thirty-five years on, competitive Amiga demo programming is still a live art form with an annual calendar.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Spaceballs, State of the Art (via Retro32)
entries.name: The Amiga demoscene
entries.what: The demoscene crystallised on the Amiga: crack intros on pirated games evolved into standalone demos, and by 1989–93 Amiga groups defined European digital youth culture — megademos, trackmos and the party circuit. Landmarks run from Enigma (Phenomena, 1991), State of the Art (Spaceballs, 1992) and Desert Dream (Kefrens, 1993) to The Black Lotus's Eon, which won Revision 2019.
entries.why: The custom chipset rewarded exactly the hardware mastery the scene celebrates, which is why 68k and AGA competitions are still marquee events. TBL, Loonies, Ghostown, Desire, Spaceballs and Elude remain active.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: ProTracker 1.1, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
entries.name: Trackers & the MOD format
entries.what: Karsten Obarski's Ultimate Soundtracker (1987) was the original sample-based tracker, built around Paula's four 8-bit DMA channels. Its lineage — NoiseTracker, then ProTracker in 1990 — produced the MOD format, and its descendants S3M, XM and IT. Olav Sørensen's pt2-clone (v1.91, July 2026) recreates ProTracker 2.3D with Amiga filter modelling.
entries.why: The Amiga's biggest single cultural export: MOD escaped the platform and shaped PC demos, game audio, early rave and jungle production, and net music culture. Also preserved live by UADE, AmigaRemix and Nectarine radio.

entries.imageCredit: LightWave render: Amiga Geek
entries.name: The Boing Ball
entries.what: The red-and-white checkered bouncing ball predates the Amiga's launch: coded overnight for the January 1984 winter CES on the Lorraine prototype, its rotation faked cheaply with colour-register cycling while a hardware-shaking "boom" thudded through the hall PA.
entries.why: Commodore replaced it with the rainbow checkmark as official branding, which is precisely why the community adopted the Boing Ball as the *real* symbol. It has appeared on AmigaOS "Boing Bags", AmigaOne branding, magazines and event logos ever since — and the Boing Ball mark is explicitly among the trademarks consolidated under Amiga Corporation in the 2026 settlement.

entries.imageCredit: Screenshot: Metro Siege / BitBeamCannon & Pixelglass
entries.name: The new games scene 2015–2026
entries.what: A genuine commercial and freeware revival: Richard Löwenstein's RESHOOT trilogy, Tower 57, Worthy, Inviyya, Black Dawn Rebirth, Creeping Me Out, Roguecraft and Roguecraft DX, Turbo Sprint, Tenebra, an assembly-accurate OutRun port, the long-awaited Metro Siege, and GRIND on dread technology — published in boxes by Bitmap Soft, poly.play, Thalamus Digital and RETREAM, with recurring AmiGameJam events feeding the pipeline.
entries.why: New Amiga games are now released more often than in the platform's final commercial years — and several are genuinely excellent rather than merely nostalgic.
entries.version: ~594 games on the itch.io Amiga tag

entries.name: Modern ports & conversions
entries.what: What fast modern hardware unlocked: Frank Wille's AmiQuake and AmiQuake2 (RTG v3.03, August 2026), Steffen Häuser's Heretic II for PiStorm-class machines (2024), Quake 2 on AmigaOS 4 via GL4ES, maintained ScummVM builds for 68k, AmigaOS 4 and MorphOS, ClassiCube on OS4, plus AGA fan conversions like Turrican II AGA and Castlevania AGA.
entries.why: PiStorm, Vampire and next-generation hardware did not just make old software faster — they made a category of software possible that the platform never had.

entries.name: Personal Paint, IGNITION & productivity
entries.what: Classic productivity, still moving: Personal Paint now licensed by A-EON with an ARM-accelerated 7.4 shipping on the A600GS (7.1 remains free on Aminet), the open-sourced IGNITION spreadsheet at v1.30 for AmigaOS 4, MediaVault for OS4 streaming, and SketchBlock for painting.
entries.why: A reminder that the Amiga was a work machine — DTP, painting, spreadsheets, video — and that some of that software is still being developed.

entries.imageCredit: Cover scan: Amiga Format issue 60 (Retro Commodore)
entries.name: Commodore bankruptcy
entries.what: Commodore International declares bankruptcy and enters liquidation. Amiga production stops; the liquidation drags on for a year.
entries.why: The event that created everything else in this atlas. From this point the platform has no manufacturer — only stewards, licensees and volunteers.

entries.name: Escom / Amiga Technologies
entries.what: German PC maker Escom wins the auction for roughly US$10–14 million, beating Dell, and forms Amiga Technologies GmbH under Petro Tyschtschenko, restarting A1200 and A4000T production. Escom itself goes bankrupt in July 1996; QuikPak builds remaining A4000Ts and a sale to VIScorp collapses.
entries.why: The first and last time anyone tried to simply resume being Commodore.

entries.name: Gateway 2000 acquisition
entries.what: Gateway buys the Commodore and Amiga assets out of the Escom bankruptcy for around US$13 million, mainly for the patent portfolio. Amiga International licenses the classic hardware; Gateway's 1999 next-generation projects under Jim Collas are cancelled.
entries.why: The moment the Amiga became primarily a patent asset rather than a product line.

entries.name: Amiga, Inc. (McEwen)
entries.what: Gateway sells the Amiga name, trademarks, OS and remaining IP — patents excluded and licensed back — to Bill McEwen and Fleecy Moss's Amino Development Corp, renamed Amiga, Inc. (Washington). Its strategy centres on AmigaDE rather than AmigaOS.
entries.why: The brand and the technology begin to diverge: the company holding the name spends the decade pointing it away from Amiga hardware.

entries.name: Hyperion contracted for AmigaOS 4
entries.what: Amiga Inc. contracts Hyperion Entertainment of Belgium — founded in 1999 by Ben Hermans and Evert Carton — to develop AmigaOS 4 for PowerPC AmigaOne boards.
entries.why: The contract that produced a real, shipping, official AmigaOS — and, eight years later, the lawsuit that defined who owns what.

entries.name: KMOS / Amiga, Inc. (Delaware)
entries.what: Amid financial trouble, Amiga Inc.'s OS-related assets pass to KMOS, Inc., which renames itself Amiga, Inc. (Delaware) in 2005.
entries.why: The Washington/Delaware duality created years of genuine legal confusion about which entity held which rights.

entries.imageCredit: Court filing: U.S. District Court / Amiga Documents
entries.name: 2009 Amiga Inc. v. Hyperion settlement
entries.what: Settling litigation begun in 2007, Hyperion receives an exclusive, perpetual, royalty-free worldwide licence to AmigaOS 3.1 to develop and market "AmigaOS 4 and subsequent versions" under the AmigaOS name, while Amiga Inc. retains the trademarks.
entries.why: The legal backbone of everything that followed — including Hyperion's later right to ship AmigaOS 3.1.4 and 3.2 for classic machines.

entries.name: A-EON Technology & AmigaKit
entries.what: A-EON Technology is founded, with AmigaKit as its retail and manufacturing arm, becoming the patron of AmigaOS 4 hardware: the X1000 (2012), X5000 (2016) and A1222 Plus, plus the Enhancer Software stack and the AmiSphere platform.
entries.why: For fifteen years, essentially all new AmigaOS 4 hardware has existed because of private patronage rather than a market.

entries.name: Cloanto acquires the OS copyrights
entries.what: Cloanto — long the publisher of Amiga Forever — acquires Amiga Inc.'s Commodore and Amiga OS copyrights covering AmigaOS 3.1 and earlier. In 2019 Battilana's C-A Acquisition Corp buys the remaining Amiga, Inc. assets including the trademarks and becomes Amiga Corporation.
entries.why: For the first time since 1994, the historic copyrights and the trademarks are consolidated under one owner who actually licenses them.

entries.name: The Hyperion litigation era
entries.what: Relations rupture as Hyperion ships AmigaOS 3.1.4 and then 3.2 for classic machines. Litigation runs in the US and Belgium from 2018, with partial settlements reported around 2021–22, alongside a separate long-running dispute with A-EON and AmigaKit over the Enhancer Software's duplicated components and the ExecSG kernel.
entries.why: It froze parts of the ecosystem for years — Retro Games Ltd publicly blamed the litigation for delaying THEA1200 past 2025.

entries.name: Hyperion under new ownership
entries.what: After the bankruptcy of Ben Hermans BV, Hyperion's largest shareholder, a court-supervised shareholders' meeting annuls that shareholding and appoints Timothy De Groote as director. (Hyperion itself was never bankrupt — only the shareholder vehicle. Widely circulated claims about Ben Hermans' personal circumstances could not be verified and should not be repeated.)
entries.why: The reset that restarted official development: AmigaOS 3.2.3 in April 2025, 4.1 FE Update 3 in October 2025, digital 3.2 in March 2026 and a new SDK in June 2026.

entries.imageCredit: Product render: Commodore
entries.name: Commodore returns
entries.what: A group of angel investors fronted by YouTuber Christian "Perifractic" Simpson acquires Commodore Corporation B.V. — holder of the remaining Commodore trademarks — for a low seven-figure sum; Simpson becomes CEO. First product: the FPGA-based Commodore 64 Ultimate from $299.99, built on Gideon Zweijtzer's Ultimate-64 technology, with first deliveries at Christmas 2025.
entries.why: Crucially, the deal includes **no Amiga rights**. Commodore and Amiga are now separately owned, and the two are frequently confused — the single most common misunderstanding in the current landscape.

entries.imageCredit: Page capture: Amiga Corporation
entries.name: The 2026 settlement
entries.what: All litigation ends. Hyperion acknowledges Amiga Corporation's ownership of the trademarks, with over twenty registrations transferring; AmigaOS 4 remains Hyperion's property with a fresh OS 3.1 source licence, exclusive rights to the AmigaOne brand, and freedom to port AmigaOS 4 to **any CPU architecture except 68k**. Hyperion's licence to sell AmigaOS 3.2/3.3 for 68k expires 31 December 2027, after which it hands the sources to Amiga Corporation and exits the classic market. Hyperion states it will complete AmigaOS 3.3 and 4.2.
entries.why: The most consequential development in decades: it ends the legal paralysis, frees AmigaOS 4 from PowerPC, and schedules the transfer of 68k stewardship. The same-day agreement also formalises the Commodore relationship and names Retro Games Ltd and Blaze Entertainment as licensees.

entries.name: Who owns what, August 2026
entries.what: Amiga trademarks (Amiga, AmigaOS, Kickstart, Workbench, Boing Ball) and the historic Commodore and Amiga software copyrights: **Amiga Corporation** (Mike Battilana). AmigaOS 4.x, and 3.2/3.3 until end-2027, plus the AmigaOne brand: **Hyperion Entertainment**. 68k AmigaOS after 2027: **Amiga Corporation**. The Commodore and C= marks: **Commodore International Corporation** — with no Amiga rights. MorphOS: the independent **MorphOS Team**. AROS: open source. The 1997-era hardware patents have expired.
entries.why: Technical lineage and corporate ownership are two different maps. Nearly every "wait, who makes the Amiga now?" confusion comes from conflating them.
